entries.9315802d4e951827881178c3b8cb3ed295a9e63a: <div sID="gen27185" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="John.7" sID="John.7"/> <div eID="gen27185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27186" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27187" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Christ's declining for some time to appear publicly in Judea, <reference osisRef="John.7.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His design to go up to Jerusalem at the feast of tabernacles, and his discourse with his kindred in Galilee concerning his going up to this feast, <reference osisRef="John.7.2-John.7.13">ver. 2-13</reference>. III. His preaching publicly in the temple at that feast. 1. In the midst of the feast, <reference osisRef="John.7.14-John.7.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. We have his discourse with the Jews, (1.) Concerning his doctrine, <reference osisRef="John.7.16-John.7.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. (2.) Concerning the crime of sabbath-breaking laid to his charge, <reference osisRef="John.7.19-John.7.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. (3.) Concerning himself, both whence he came and whither he was going, <reference osisRef="John.7.25-John.7.36">ver. 25-36</reference>. 2. On the last day of he feast. (1.) His gracious invitation to poor souls to come to him, <reference osisRef="John.7.37-John.7.39">ver. 37-39</reference>. (2.) The reception that it met with. [1.] Many of the people disputed about it, <reference osisRef="John.7.40-John.7.44">ver. 40-44</reference>. [2.] The chief priests would have brought him into trouble for it, but were first disappointed by their officers (<reference osisRef="John.7.45-John.7.49">ver. 45-49</reference>) and then silenced by one of their own court, <reference osisRef="John.7.50-John.7.53">ver. 50-53</reference>.
entries.4cb60967787ae6822c09e9eee6b92a9b9a8a3583: <div eID="gen27187" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27186" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with His Brethren; The Rumours Respecting Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand. 3 His brethren therefore said unto him, Depart hence, and go into Judæa, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest. <hi type="super">4</hi> For <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no man <hi type="italic">that</hi> doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, show thyself to the world. <hi type="super">5</hi> For neither did his brethren believe in him. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready. <hi type="super">7</hi> The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil. <hi type="super">8</hi> Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come. <hi type="super">9</hi> When he had said these words unto them, he abode <hi type="italic">still</hi> in Galilee. <hi type="super">10</hi> But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then the Jews sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he? <hi type="super">12</hi> And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people. <hi type="super">13</hi> Howbeit no man spake openly of him for fear of the Jews. <div eID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The reason given why Christ spent more of his time in Galilee than in Judea (<reference osisRef="John.7.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">because the Jews,</hi> the people in Judea and Jerusalem, sought to <hi type="italic">kill him,</hi> for curing the impotent man on the sabbath day, <reference osisRef="John.5.16">ch. v. 16</reference>. They thought to be the death of him, either by a popular tumult or by a legal prosecution, in consideration of which he kept at a distance in another part of the country, very much out of the lines of Jerusalem's communication. It is not said, He <hi type="italic">durst not,</hi> but, He <hi type="italic">would not,</hi> walk in Jewry; it was not through fear and cowardice that he declined it, but in <hi type="italic">prudence,</hi> because his hour was not yet come. Note, 1. Gospel light is justly <hi type="italic">taken away</hi> from those that endeavour to extinguish it. Christ will withdraw from those that drive him from them, will hide his face from those that spit in it, and justly shut up his bowels from those who spurn at them. 2. In times of imminent peril it is not only <hi type="italic">allowable,</hi> but <hi type="italic">advisable,</hi> to <hi type="italic">withdraw</hi> and <hi type="italic">abscond</hi> for our own safety and preservation, and to choose the service of those places which are least perilous, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">Matt. x. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> and not till <hi type="italic">then,</hi> we are called to expose and lay down our lives, when we cannot save them without sin. 3. If the providence of God casts persons of <hi type="italic">merit</hi> into places of obscurity and little note, it must not be thought strange; it was the lot of our Master himself. He who was fit to have sat in the highest of Moses's seats willingly walked in Galilee among the ordinary sort of people. Observe, He did not sit still in Galilee, nor bury himself alive there, but <hi type="italic">walked;</hi> he went about doing good. When we cannot do <hi type="italic">what</hi> and <hi type="italic">where</hi> we <hi type="italic">would,</hi> we must do <hi type="italic">what</hi> and <hi type="italic">where</hi> we <hi type="italic">can.</hi> <div eID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> II. The approach of the <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.2">v. 2</reference>), one of the three solemnities which called for the personal attendance of all the males at Jerusalem; see the institution of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Lev. xxiii. 34</reference>, &c., and the revival of it after a long disuse, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.14">Neh. viii. 14</reference>. It was intended to be both a <hi type="italic">memorial</hi> of the tabernacle state of Israel in the wilderness, and a <hi type="italic">figure</hi> of the tabernacle state of God's spiritual Israel in this world. This feast, which was instituted so many hundred years before, was still religiously observed. Note, Divine institutions are never antiquated, nor go out of date, by length of time: nor must wilderness mercies ever be forgotten. But it is called the <hi type="italic">Jews' feast,</hi> because it was now shortly to be <hi type="italic">abolished,</hi> as a mere Jewish thing, and left to them that <hi type="italic">served the tabernacle.</hi> <div eID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's discourse with his <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> some of his kindred, whether by his mother or his supposed father is not certain; but they were such as pretended to have an interest in him, and therefore interposed to advise him in his conduct. And observe, <div eID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> 1. Their ambition and vain-glory in urging him to make a more public appearance than he did: "<hi type="italic">Depart hence,</hi>" said they, "<hi type="italic">and go into Judea</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.3">v. 3</reference>), where thou wilt make a better figure than thou canst here." <div eID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> (1.) They give two reasons for this advice: [1.] That it would be an encouragement to those in and about Jerusalem who had a respect for him; for, expecting his temporal kingdom, the royal seat of which they concluded must be at Jerusalem, they would have had the disciples <hi type="italic">there</hi> particularly countenanced, and thought the time he spent among his Galilean disciples wasted and thrown away, and his miracles turning to no account unless those at Jerusalem saw them. Or, "That <hi type="italic">thy disciples,</hi> all of them in general, who will be gathered at Jerusalem to keep the feast, may <hi type="italic">see thy works,</hi> and not, as here, a few at one time and a few at another." [2.] That it would be for the advancement of his name and honour: <hi type="italic">There is no man that does any thing in secret</hi> if he himself <hi type="italic">seeks to be known</hi> openly. They took it for granted that Christ sought to make himself known, and therefore thought it absurd for him to conceal his miracles: "<hi type="italic">If thou do these things,</hi> if thou be so well able to gain the applause of the people and the approbation of the rulers by thy miracles, venture abroad, and <hi type="italic">show thyself to the world.</hi> Supported with these credentials, thou canst not fail of acceptance, and therefore it is high time to set up for an interest, and to think of being <hi type="italic">great.</hi>" <div eID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> (2.) One would not think there was any harm in this advice, and yet the evangelist noted it is an evidence of their infidelity: <hi type="italic">For neither did his brethren believe in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">v. 5</reference>), if they had, they would not have said this. Observe, [1.] It was an honour to be of the kindred of Christ, but no <hi type="italic">saving</hi> honour; they that hear his word and keep it are the kindred he values. Surely grace runs in no blood in the world, when not in that of Christ's family. [2.] It was a sign that Christ did not aim at any secular interest, for then his kindred would have struck in with him, and he would have secured them first. [3.] There were those who were akin to Christ according to the flesh who did believe in him (three of the twelve were <hi type="italic">his brethren</hi>), and yet others, as nearly allied to him as they, did not believe in him. Many that have the same external privileges and advantages do not make the same use of them. But, <div eID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> (3.) What was there amiss in the advice which they gave him? I answer, [1.] It was a piece of presumption for them to prescribe to Christ, and to teach him what measures to take; it was a sign that they <hi type="italic">did not believe him</hi> able to guide them, when they did not think him sufficient to guide himself. [2.] They discovered a great carelessness about his safety, when they would have him go to Judea, where they knew the Jews sought to kill him. Those that believed in him, and loved him, dissuaded him from Judea, <reference osisRef="John.11.8">ch. xi. 8</reference>. [3.] Some think they hoped that if his miracles were wrought at Jerusalem the Pharisees and rulers would try them, and discover some cheat in them, which would justify their unbelief. So. Dr. Whitby. [4.] Perhaps they were weary of his company in Galilee (for <hi type="italic">are not all these that speak Galileans?</hi>) and this was, in effect, a desire that he would <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts.</hi> [5.] They causelessly insinuate that he neglected his disciples, and denied them such a <hi type="italic">sight of his works</hi> as was necessary to the support of their faith. [6.] They tacitly reproach him as <hi type="italic">mean-spirited,</hi> that he durst not enter the lists with the great men, nor trust himself upon the stage of public action, which, if he had any courage and <hi type="italic">greatness of soul,</hi> he would do, and not sneak thus and skulk in a corner; thus Christ's humility, and his humiliation, and the small figure which his religion has usually made in the world, have been often turned to the reproach of both <hi type="italic">him</hi> and <hi type="italic">it.</hi> [7.] They seem to question the truth of the miracles he wrought, in saying, "<hi type="italic">If thou do these things,</hi> if they will bear the test of a public scrutiny in the courts above, produce them there." [8.] They think Christ altogether such a one as themselves, as subject as they to worldly policy, and as desirous as they to <hi type="italic">make a fair show in the flesh;</hi> whereas he sought not honour from men. [9.] Self was at the bottom of all; they hoped, if he would make himself as great as he might, they, being his kinsmen, should share in his honour, and have respect paid them for his sake. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Many carnal people go to public ordinances, to worship at the feast, only to <hi type="italic">show themselves,</hi> and all their care is to make a <hi type="italic">good appearance,</hi> to present themselves handsomely to the world. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Many that seem to seek Christ's honour do really therein seek their own, and make it serve a turn for themselves. <div eID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> 2. The prudence and humility of our Lord Jesus, which appeared in his answer to the advice his brethren gave him, <reference osisRef="John.7.6-John.7.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Though there were so many base insinuations in it, he answered them mildly. Note, Even that which is said without <hi type="italic">reason</hi> should be answered without <hi type="italic">passion;</hi> we should learn of our Master to reply with meekness even to that which is most <hi type="italic">impertinent</hi> and <hi type="italic">imperious,</hi> and, where it is easy to find much amiss, to seem not to see it, and wink at the affront. They expected Christ's company with them to the feast, perhaps hoping he would bear their charges: but here, <div eID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows the difference between himself and them, in two things:—[1.] His <hi type="italic">time</hi> was <hi type="italic">set,</hi> so was not <hi type="italic">theirs: My time is not yet come, but your time is always ready.</hi> Understand it of the time of his going up to the feast. It was an indifferent thing to them when they went, for they had nothing of moment to do either where they were, to <hi type="italic">detain</hi> them <hi type="italic">there,</hi> or where they were going, to <hi type="italic">hasten</hi> them <hi type="italic">thither;</hi> but every minute of Christ's time was precious, and had its own particular business allotted to it. He had some work yet to do in Galilee before he left the country: in the harmony of the gospels betwixt this <hi type="italic">motion</hi> made by his kindred and his <hi type="italic">going up</hi> to this feast comes in the story of his sending forth the seventy disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Luke x. 1</reference>, &c.), which was an affair of very great consequence; his time is <hi type="italic">not yet,</hi> for that must be done first. Those who live useless lives have <hi type="italic">their time always ready;</hi> they can go and come when they please. But those whose <hi type="italic">time</hi> is filled up with <hi type="italic">duty</hi> will often find themselves <hi type="italic">straitened,</hi> and they have <hi type="italic">not yet time</hi> for that which others can do <hi type="italic">at any time.</hi> Those who are made the servants of God, as all men are, and who have made themselves the servants of all, as all useful men have, must not expect not covet to be <hi type="italic">masters of their own time.</hi> The confinement of business is a thousand times better than the liberty of idleness. Or, it may be meant of the <hi type="italic">time</hi> of his appearing publicly at Jerusalem; Christ, who knows all men and all things, knew that the best and most proper time for it would be about the <hi type="italic">middle of the feast.</hi> We, who are ignorant and short-sighted, are apt to prescribe to him, and to think he should deliver his people, and so show himself now. The present time is <hi type="italic">our</hi> time, but he is fittest to judge, and, it may be, <hi type="italic">his time is not yet come;</hi> his people are not yet ready for deliverance, nor his enemies ripe for ruin; let us therefore wait with patience for <hi type="italic">his time,</hi> for all he does will be most glorious in its season. [2.] His <hi type="italic">life</hi> was <hi type="italic">sought,</hi> so was not <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.7">v. 7</reference>. They, in <hi type="italic">showing themselves</hi> to the world, did not expose themselves: "<hi type="italic">The world cannot hate you,</hi> for you are <hi type="italic">of the world,</hi> its children, its servants, and in with its interests; and no doubt the world will <hi type="italic">love its own;</hi>" see <reference osisRef="John.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>. Unholy souls, whom the holy God <hi type="italic">cannot love,</hi> the world that lies in wickedness <hi type="italic">cannot hate;</hi> but Christ, in showing himself to the world, laid himself open to the greatest danger; for <hi type="italic">me it hateth.</hi> Christ was not only <hi type="italic">slighted,</hi> as inconsiderable in the world (<hi type="italic">the world knew him not),</hi> but <hi type="italic">hated,</hi> as if he had been hurtful to the world; thus ill was he requited for his love to the world: reigning sin is a rooted antipathy and enmity to Christ. But why did the world hate Christ? What evil had he done to it? Had he, like Alexander, under colour of conquering it, laid it waste? "No, but because" (saith he) "<hi type="italic">I testify of it, that the works of it are evil.</hi>" Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The works of an evil world are <hi type="italic">evil works;</hi> as the tree is, so are the fruits: it is a dark world, and an apostate world, and its works are works of darkness and rebellion. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Our Lord Jesus, both by himself and by his ministers, did and will both discover and testify against the evil works of this wicked world. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a great uneasiness and provocation to the world to be convicted of the evil of its works. It is for the honour of virtue and piety that those who are impious and vicious do not care for hearing of it, for their own consciences make them <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> of the turpitude there is <hi type="italic">in</hi> sin and <hi type="italic">afraid</hi> of the punishment that follows <hi type="italic">after</hi> sin. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Whatever is <hi type="italic">pretended,</hi> the <hi type="italic">real</hi> cause of the world's enmity to the gospel is the testimony it bears against sin and sinners. Christ's witnesses by their doctrine and conversation <hi type="italic">torment</hi> those that dwell on the earth, and therefore are treated so barbarously, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. But it is better to incur the world's hatred, by testifying against its wickedness, than gain its good-will by going down the stream with it. <div eID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> (2.) He dismisses them, with a design to stay behind for some time in Galilee (<reference osisRef="John.7.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go you up to this feast, I go not up yet.</hi> [1.] He allows their going to the feast, though they were carnal and hypocritical in it. Note, Even those who go not to holy ordinances with right affections and sincere intentions must not be hindered nor discouraged from going; who knows but they may be wrought upon there? [2.] He denies them his company when they went to the feast, because they were carnal and hypocritical. Those who go to ordinances for ostentation, or to serve some secular purpose, go without Christ, and will speed accordingly. How sad is the condition of that man, though he reckon himself akin to Christ, to whom he saith, "<hi type="italic">Go up</hi> to such an ordinance, Go pray, Go hear the word, Go receive the sacrament, but <hi type="italic">I go not up</hi> with thee? <hi type="italic">Go thou</hi> and appear before God, but I will not appear <hi type="italic">for thee,</hi>" as <reference osisRef="Exod.33.1-Exod.33.3">Exod. xxxiii. 1-3</reference>. But, if the presence of Christ go not with us, to what purpose should we go up? <hi type="italic">Go you up, I go not up.</hi> When we are going to, or coming from, solemn ordinances, it becomes us to be careful what company we <hi type="italic">have</hi> and <hi type="italic">choose,</hi> and to avoid that which is vain and carnal, lest the coal of good affections be quenched by corrupt communication. <hi type="italic">I go not up yet to this feast;</hi> he does not say, I will not go up at all, but not yet. There may be reasons for deferring a particular duty, which yet must not be wholly omitted or laid aside; see <reference osisRef="Num.9.6-Num.9.11">Num. ix. 6-11</reference>. The reason he gives is, <hi type="italic">My time is not yet fully come.</hi> Note, Our Lord Jesus is very exact and punctual in knowing and keeping his time, and, as it was the time <hi type="italic">fixed,</hi> so it was the <hi type="italic">best</hi> time. <div eID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's continuance in Galilee till his <hi type="italic">full time</hi> was come, <reference osisRef="John.7.9">v. 9</reference>. He, saying these things to them (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tauta de eipon</hi></hi>) <hi type="italic">abode still in Galilee;</hi> because of this discourse he continued there; for, (1.) He would not be influenced by those who advised him to seek honour from men, nor go along with those who put him upon making a figure; he would not seem to countenance the temptation. (2.) He would not depart from his own purpose. He had said, upon a clear foresight and mature deliberation, that he would not go up yet to this feast, and therefore he abode still in Galilee. It becomes the followers of Christ thus to be <hi type="italic">steady,</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">use lightness.</hi> <div eID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> 4. His going up to the feast when his time was come. Observe, (1.) <hi type="italic">When</hi> he went: <hi type="italic">When his brethren were gone up.</hi> He would not go up <hi type="italic">with them,</hi> lest they should make a noise and disturbance, under pretence of <hi type="italic">showing him to the world;</hi> whereas it agreed both with the prediction and with his spirit not to <hi type="italic">strive nor cry,</hi> nor let his <hi type="italic">voice be heard in the streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.2">Isa. xlii. 2</reference>. But he went up <hi type="italic">after them.</hi> We may lawfully join in the same religious worship with those with whom we should yet decline an intimate acquaintance and converse; for the blessing of ordinances depends upon the grace of God, and not upon the grace of our fellow-worshippers. His carnal brethren went up <hi type="italic">first,</hi> and then he went. Note, In the external performances of religion it is possible that formal hypocrites may <hi type="italic">get the start</hi> of those that are sincere. Many come <hi type="italic">first to the temple</hi> who are brought thither by vain-glory, and go thence unjustified, as he, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>. It is not, Who comes <hi type="italic">first?</hi> that will be the question, but, Who comes <hi type="italic">fittest?</hi> If we bring our hearts <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> it is no matter who gets <hi type="italic">before us.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">How</hi> he went, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">os en krypto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a s if he were hiding himself: not openly, but as it were in secret,</hi> rather for fear of <hi type="italic">giving offence</hi> than of <hi type="italic">receiving injury.</hi> He went up to the feast, because it was an opportunity of honouring God and doing good; but he went up as it were in secret, because he would not provoke the government. Note, Provided the work of God be done effectually, it is best done when done with <hi type="italic">least noise.</hi> The kingdom of God need not come <hi type="italic">with observation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.20">Luke xvii. 20</reference>. We may do the work of God <hi type="italic">privately,</hi> and yet not do it <hi type="italic">deceitfully.</hi> <div eID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> 5. The great expectation that there was of him among the Jews at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="John.7.11-John.7.14">v. 11-14</reference>. Having formerly come up to the feasts, and signalized himself by the miracles he wrought, he had made himself the subject of much discourse and observation. <div eID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27202" type="x-p"/> (1.) They could not but think of him (<reference osisRef="John.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Jews sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he?</hi> [1.] The common people longed to see him there, that they might have their curiosity gratified with the sight of his person and miracles. They did not think it worth while to go to him into Galilee, though if they had they would not have lost their labour, but they hoped the feast would bring him to Jerusalem, and then they should see him. If an opportunity of acquaintance with Christ come to their door, they can like it well enough. They <hi type="italic">sought him at the feast.</hi> When we attend upon God in his holy ordinances, we should seek Christ in them, seek him at the gospel feasts. Those who would <hi type="italic">see</hi> Christ at a feast must <hi type="italic">seek</hi> him there. Or, [2.] Perhaps it was his enemies that were thus waiting an opportunity to seize him, and, if possible, to put an effectual stop to his progress. They said, <hi type="italic">Where is he?</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pou esin ekeinos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">where is that fellow?</hi> Thus scornfully and contemptibly do they speak of him. When they should have welcomed the feast as an opportunity of serving God, they were glad of it as an opportunity of persecuting Christ. Thus Saul hoped to slay David at the new moon, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27">1 Sam. xx. 27</reference>. Those who seek <hi type="italic">opportunity to sin</hi> in solemn assemblies for religious worship profane God's ordinances to the last degree, and defy him upon his own ground; it is like striking <hi type="italic">within the verge of the court.</hi> <div eID="gen27202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> (2.) The people differed much in their sentiments concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was much murmuring,</hi> or <hi type="italic">muttering</hi> rather, <hi type="italic">among the people concerning him.</hi> The enmity of the rulers against Christ, and their enquiries after him, caused him to be so much the more talked of and observed among the people. This ground the gospel of Christ has got by the opposition made to it, that it has been the more enquired into, and, by being <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi> it has come to be every where <hi type="italic">spoken of,</hi> and by this means has been spread the further, and the merits of his cause have been the more <hi type="italic">searched into.</hi> This murmuring was not <hi type="italic">against</hi> Christ, but <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> him; some murmured at the rulers, because they did not countenance and encourage him: others murmured at them, because they did not silence and restrain him. Some murmured that he had so great an interest in Galilee; others, that he had so little interest in Jerusalem. Note, Christ and his religion have been, and will be, the subject of much controversy and debate, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.51-Luke.12.52">Luke xii. 51, 52</reference>. If all would agree to entertain Christ as they ought, there would be perfect peace; but, when some receive the light and others resolve against it, there will be murmuring. The <hi type="italic">bones in the valley,</hi> while they were <hi type="italic">dead</hi> and <hi type="italic">dry,</hi> lay quiet; but when it was said unto them, <hi type="italic">Live,</hi> there was <hi type="italic">a noise</hi> and <hi type="italic">a shaking,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.7">Ezek. xxxvii. 7</reference>. But the noise and rencounter of liberty and business are preferable, surely, to the silence and agreement of a prison. Now what were the sentiments of the people concerning him? [1.] Some said, <hi type="italic">he is a good man.</hi> This was a truth, but it was far short of being the <hi type="italic">whole truth.</hi> He was not only a <hi type="italic">good man,</hi> but more than a man, he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> Many who have no <hi type="italic">ill</hi> thoughts of Christ have yet <hi type="italic">low</hi> thoughts of him, and scarcely honour him, even when they speak well of him, because they do not <hi type="italic">say enough;</hi> yet indeed it was his honour, and the reproach of those who persecuted him, that even those who would not believe him to be the Messiah could not but own he was a <hi type="italic">good man.</hi> [2.] Others said, <hi type="italic">Nay, but he deceiveth the people;</hi> if this had been true, he had been a very bad man. The doctrine he preached was sound, and could not be contested; his miracles were real, and could not be disproved; his conversation was manifestly holy and good; and yet it must be taken for granted, notwithstanding, that there was some undiscovered cheat at the bottom, because it was the interest of the chief priests to oppose him and run him down. Such murmuring as there was among the Jews concerning Christ there is still among us: the Socinians say, <hi type="italic">He is a good man,</hi> and further they say not; the <hi type="italic">deists</hi> will not allow this, but say, <hi type="italic">He deceived the people.</hi> Thus some depreciate him, others abuse him, but <hi type="italic">great is the truth.</hi> [3.] They were frightened by their superiors from speaking much of him (<reference osisRef="John.7.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">No man spoke openly of him, for fear of the Jews.</hi> Either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They durst not openly speak <hi type="italic">well</hi> of him. While any one was at liberty to censure and reproach him, none durst vindicate him. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They durst not speak <hi type="italic">at all</hi> of him openly. Because nothing could justly be said <hi type="italic">against</hi> him, they would not suffer any thing to be said <hi type="italic">of</hi> him. It was a crime to name him. Thus many have aimed to suppress truth, under colour of silencing disputes about it, and would have all talk of religion hushed, in hopes thereby to bury in oblivion religion itself.
entries.9b2e84784b35d9ae970d77f14424fdd86e2405e2: <div eID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ at the Feast of Tabernacles.</title> <div sID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Now about the midst of the feast Jesus went up into the temple, and taught. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the Jews marvelled, saying, How knoweth this man letters, having never learned? <hi type="super">16</hi> Jesus answered them, and said, My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me. <hi type="super">17</hi> If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or <hi type="italic">whether</hi> I speak of myself. <hi type="super">18</hi> He that speaketh of himself seeketh his own glory: but he that seeketh his glory that sent him, the same is true, and no unrighteousness is in him. <hi type="super">19</hi> Did not Moses give you the law, and <hi type="italic">yet</hi> none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me? <hi type="super">20</hi> The people answered and said, Thou hast a devil: who goeth about to kill thee? <hi type="super">21</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, I have done one work, and ye all marvel. <hi type="super">22</hi> Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; (not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man. <hi type="super">23</hi> If a man on the sabbath day receive circumcision, that the law of Moses should not be broken; are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day? <hi type="super">24</hi> Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then said some of them of Jerusalem, Is not this he, whom they seek to kill? <hi type="super">26</hi> But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ? <hi type="super">27</hi> Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then cried Jesus in the temple as he taught, saying, Ye both know me, and ye know whence I am: and I am not come of myself, but he that sent me is true, whom ye know not. <hi type="super">29</hi> But I know him: for I am from him, and he hath sent me. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then they sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come. <hi type="super">31</hi> And many of the people believed on him, and said, When Christ cometh, will he do more miracles than these which this <hi type="italic">man</hi> hath done? <hi type="super">32</hi> The Pharisees heard that the people murmured such things concerning him; and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to take him. <hi type="super">33</hi> Then said Jesus unto them, Yet a little while am I with you, and <hi type="italic">then</hi> I go unto him that sent me. <hi type="super">34</hi> Ye shall seek me, and shall not find <hi type="italic">me:</hi> and where I am, <hi type="italic">thither</hi> ye cannot come. <hi type="super">35</hi> Then said the Jews among themselves, Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles? <hi type="super">36</hi> What <hi type="italic">manner of</hi> saying is this that he said, Ye shall seek me, and shall not find <hi type="italic">me:</hi> and where I am, <hi type="italic">thither</hi> ye cannot come? <div eID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27205" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Christ's public preaching in the temple (<reference osisRef="John.7.14">v. 14</reference>): He <hi type="italic">went up into the temple, and taught,</hi> according to his custom when he was at Jerusalem. His business was to preach the gospel of the kingdom, and he did it in every place of concourse. His sermon is not recorded, because, probably, it was to the same purport with the sermons he had preached in Galilee, which were recorded by the other evangelists. For the gospel is the same to the <hi type="italic">plain</hi> and to the <hi type="italic">polite.</hi> But that which is observable here is that it was <hi type="italic">about the midst of the feast;</hi> the fourth or fifth day of the eight. Whether he did not come up to Jerusalem till the middle of the feast, or whether he came up at the beginning, but kept private till now, is not certain. But, <hi type="italic">Query,</hi> Why did he not go to the temple <hi type="italic">sooner,</hi> to preach? <hi type="italic">Answer,</hi> 1. Because the people would have more leisure to hear him, and, it might be hoped, would be better disposed to hear him, when they had spent some days in their booths, as they did at the feast of tabernacles. 2. Because he would choose to appear when both his friends and his enemies had done looking for him; and so give a specimen of the method he would observe in his appearances, which is to come at midnight, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Matt. xxv. 6</reference>. But why did he appear thus publicly now? Surely it was to <hi type="italic">shame</hi> his persecutors, the chief priests and elders. (1.) By showing that, though they were very bitter against him, yet he did not fear them, nor their power. See <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7-Isa.50.8">Isa. l. 7, 8</reference>. (2.) By taking their work out of their hands. Their office was to teach the people in the temple, and particularly at the <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.8.17-Neh.8.18">Neh. viii. 17, 18</reference>. But they either did not teach them at all or taught for doctrines the commandments of men, and therefore he goes up to the temple and teaches the people. When the shepherds of Israel made a prey of the flock it was time for the chief Shepherd to appear, as was promised. <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.22-Ezek.34.23">Ezek. xxxiv. 22, 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal. iii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen27205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27206" type="x-p"/> II. His discourse with the Jews hereupon; and the conference is reducible to four heads: <div eID="gen27206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27207" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning <hi type="italic">his doctrine.</hi> See here, <div eID="gen27207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> (1.) How the Jews <hi type="italic">admired</hi> it (<reference osisRef="John.7.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">They marvelled,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?</hi> Observe here, [1.] That our Lord Jesus was not educated in the schools of the prophets, or at the feet of the rabbin; not only did not travel for learning, as the philosophers did, but did not make any use of the schools and academies in his own country. Moses was taught the learning of the Egyptians, but Christ was not taught so much as the learning of the Jews; having received the Spirit <hi type="italic">without measure,</hi> he needed not receive any knowledge <hi type="italic">from man, or by man.</hi> At the time of Christ's appearing, learning flourished both in the Roman empire and in the Jewish church more than in any age before or since, and in such a time of enquiry Christ chose to establish his religion, not in an illiterate age, lest it should look like a design to impose upon the world; yet he himself studied not the learning then in vogue. [2.] That Christ <hi type="italic">had letters,</hi> though he had never <hi type="italic">learned</hi> them; was mighty in the scriptures, though he never had any doctor of the law for his tutor. It is necessary that Christ's ministers should have <hi type="italic">learning,</hi> as he had; and since they cannot expect to have it as he had it, by inspiration, they must take pains to get it in an ordinary way. [3.] That Christ's having learning, though he had not been taught it, made him truly great and wonderful; the Jews speak of it here with wonder. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some, it is likely, took notice of it to his honour: He that had no human learning, and yet so far excelled all that had, certainly must be endued with a divine knowledge. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Others, probably, mentioned it in disparagement and contempt of him: Whatever he <hi type="italic">seems</hi> to have, he cannot really have any true learning, for he was never at the university, nor took his degree. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Some perhaps suggested that he had got his learning by magic arts, or some unlawful means or other. Since they know not how he could be a scholar, they will think him a conjurer. <div eID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he <hi type="italic">asserted</hi> concerning it; three things:— <div eID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27210" type="x-p"/> [1.] That his <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> is <hi type="italic">divine</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.</hi> They were offended because he undertook to <hi type="italic">teach</hi> though he had never learned, in answer to which he tells them that his doctrine was such as was not to be <hi type="italic">learned,</hi> for it was not the product of <hi type="italic">human thought</hi> and natural powers enlarged and elevated by reading and conversation, but it was a <hi type="italic">divine revelation.</hi> As God, equal with the Father, he might truly have said, <hi type="italic">My doctrine is mine, and his that sent me;</hi> but being now in his estate of humiliation, and being, as Mediator, God's servant, it was more congruous to say, "<hi type="italic">My doctrine is not mine,</hi> not mine only, nor mine originally, as man and mediator, but <hi type="italic">his that sent me;</hi> it does not centre in myself, nor lead ultimately to myself, but to him that sent me." God had promised concerning the great prophet that he would <hi type="italic">put his words into his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">Deut. xviii. 18</reference>), to which Christ seems here to refer. Note, It is the comfort of those who embrace Christ's doctrine, and the condemnation of those who reject it, that it is a divine doctrine: it is <hi type="italic">of God and not of man.</hi> <div eID="gen27210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the most competent judges of the truth and divine authority of Christ's doctrine are those that with a sincere and upright heart desire and endeavour to do the will of God (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">If any man be willing to do the will of God,</hi> have his will melted into the <hi type="italic">will of God, he shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God or whether I speak of myself.</hi> Observe here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What the question is, concerning the doctrine of Christ, <hi type="italic">whether it be of God</hi> or no; whether the gospel be a divine revelation or an imposture. Christ himself was willing to have his doctrine enquired into, whether it were of God or no, much more should his ministers; and we are concerned to examine what grounds we go upon, for, if we be deceived, we are miserably deceived. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Who are likely to succeed in this search: those that <hi type="italic">do the will of God,</hi> at least are desirous to do it. Now see, 1. Who they are that <hi type="italic">will do the will of God.</hi> They are such as are <hi type="italic">impartial</hi> in their enquiries concerning the will of God, and are not biassed by any lust or interest, and such as are resolved by the grace of God, when they find out what the will of God is, to conform to it. They are such as have an honest principle of regard to God, and are truly desirous to glorify and please him. 2. Whence it is that such a one shall know of the truth of Christ's doctrine. (1.) Christ has promised to <hi type="italic">give knowledge</hi> to such; he hath said, <hi type="italic">He shall know,</hi> and he can give an understanding. Those who improve the light they have, and carefully live up to it, shall be secured by divine grace from destructive mistakes. (2.) They are disposed and prepared to <hi type="italic">receive</hi> that knowledge. He that is inclined to submit to the rules of the divine law is disposed to admit the rays of divine light. <hi type="italic">To him that has</hi> shall be given; those have a <hi type="italic">good understanding</hi> that <hi type="italic">do his commandments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Ps. cxi. 10</reference>. Those who <hi type="italic">resemble</hi> God are most likely to <hi type="italic">understand</hi> him. <div eID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> [3.] That hereby it appeared that Christ, as a teacher, did not speak <hi type="italic">of himself,</hi> because he did not seek himself, <reference osisRef="John.7.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> See here the character of a deceiver: he <hi type="italic">seeketh his own glory,</hi> which is a sign that he <hi type="italic">speaks of himself,</hi> as the false Christs and false prophets did. Here is the description of the <hi type="italic">cheat:</hi> they <hi type="italic">speak of themselves,</hi> and have no commission nor instructions from God; no warrant but their own will, no inspiration but their own imagination, their own policy and artifice. Ambassadors <hi type="italic">speak not of themselves;</hi> those ministers disclaim that character who glory in this that they <hi type="italic">speak of themselves.</hi> But see the discovery of the cheat; by this their pretensions are disproved, they consult purely <hi type="italic">their own glory;</hi> self-seekers are self-speakers. Those who speak <hi type="italic">from God</hi> will speak <hi type="italic">for God,</hi> and for his glory; those who aim at their own preferment and interest make it to appear that they had no commission form God. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> See the contrary character Christ gives of himself and his doctrine: <hi type="italic">He that seeks his glory that sent him,</hi> as I do, makes it to appear that <hi type="italic">he is true.</hi> 1. He was <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> Those teachers, and those only, who are sent of God, are to be received and entertained by us. Those who bring a divine message must prove a divine mission, either by special revelation or by regular institution. 2. He <hi type="italic">sought the glory of God.</hi> It was both the tendency of his doctrine and the tenour of his whole conversation to <hi type="italic">glorify God.</hi> 3. This was a proof that he was <hi type="italic">true,</hi> and there was <hi type="italic">no unrighteousness in him.</hi> False teachers are most <hi type="italic">unrighteous;</hi> they are unjust to God whose name they abuse, and unjust to the souls of men whom they impose upon. There cannot be a greater piece of unrighteousness than this. But Christ made it appear that he was <hi type="italic">true,</hi> that he was really what he said he was, that there was <hi type="italic">no unrighteousness</hi> in him, no falsehood in his doctrine, no fallacy nor fraud in his dealings with us. <div eID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27213" type="x-p"/> 2. They discourse concerning the <hi type="italic">crime</hi> that was laid to his charge for curing the impotent man, and bidding him carry his bed on the sabbath day, for which they had formerly prosecuted him, and which was still the pretence of their enmity to him. <div eID="gen27213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27214" type="x-p"/> (1.) He argues against them by way of <hi type="italic">recrimination,</hi> convicting them of far worse practices, <reference osisRef="John.7.19">v. 19</reference>. How could they for shame censure him for a breach of the law of Moses, when they themselves were such notorious breakers of it? <hi type="italic">Did not Moses give you the law?</hi> And it was their privilege that they had the law, no nation had such a law; but it was their wickedness that <hi type="italic">none of them kept the law,</hi> that they rebelled against it, and lived contrary to it. Many that have the law given them, when they have it do not keep it. Their neglect of the law was universal: <hi type="italic">None of you keepeth</hi> it: neither those of them that were in <hi type="italic">posts of honour,</hi> who should have been most <hi type="italic">knowing,</hi> nor those who were in <hi type="italic">posts of subjection,</hi> who should have been most <hi type="italic">obedient.</hi> They boasted of the law, and pretended a zeal for it, and were enraged at Christ for seeming to transgress it, and yet none of them kept it; like those who say that they are for the church, and yet never go to church. It was an aggravation of their wickedness, in persecuting Christ for breaking the law, that they themselves did not keep it: "<hi type="italic">None of you keepeth the law,</hi> why then go ye about to kill me for not keeping it?" Note, Those are commonly most censorious of others who are most faulty themselves. Thus hypocrites, who are forward to pull a mote out of their brother's eye, are not aware of a beam in their own. <hi type="italic">Why go ye about to kill me?</hi> Some take this as the evidence of their not keeping the law: "<hi type="italic">You keep not the law;</hi> if you did, you would understand yourselves better than to go about to kill me for doing a good work." Those that support themselves and their interest by persecution and violence, whatever they pretend (though they may call themselves <hi type="italic">custodes utriusque tabulæ—the guardians of both tables</hi>), are not keepers of the law of God. Chemnitius understands this as a reason why it was time to supersede the law of Moses by the gospel, because the law was found insufficient to <hi type="italic">restrain sin:</hi> "Moses gave you the law, but you do not keep it, nor are kept by it from the greatest wickedness; there is therefore need of a clearer light and better law to be brought in; why then do you aim to kill me for introducing it?" <div eID="gen27214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27215" type="x-p"/> Here the <hi type="italic">people</hi> rudely interrupted him in his discourse, and contradicted what he said (<reference osisRef="John.7.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou has a devil; who goes about to kill thee?</hi> This intimates, [1.] The <hi type="italic">good opinion</hi> they had of their rulers, who, they think, would never attempt so atrocious a thing as to kill him; no, such a veneration they had for their elders and chief priests that they would swear for them they would do no harm to an innocent man. Probably the rulers had their little emissaries among the people who suggested this to them; many deny that wickedness which at the same time they are contriving. [2.] The <hi type="italic">ill opinion</hi> they had of our Lord Jesus: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast a devil,</hi> thou art possessed with a lying spirit, and art a <hi type="italic">bad man</hi> for saying so;" so some: or rather, "Thou art melancholy, and art a <hi type="italic">weak man;</hi> thou frightenest thyself with causeless fears, as hypochondriacal people are apt to do." Not only open frenzies, but silent melancholies, were then commonly imputed to the power of Satan. "Thou art crazed, has a distempered brain." Let us not think it strange if the best of men are put under the worst of characters. To this vile calumny our Saviour returns no direct answer, but seems as if he took no notice of it. Note, Those who would be like Christ must put up with affronts, and pass by the indignities and injuries done them; must not <hi type="italic">regard</hi> them, much less <hi type="italic">resent</hi> them, and least of all <hi type="italic">revenge</hi> them. <hi type="italic">I, as a deaf man, heard not.</hi> When Christ was <hi type="italic">reviled,</hi> he <hi type="italic">reviled not again,</hi> <div eID="gen27215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27216" type="x-p"/> (2.) He argues by way of appeal and vindication. <div eID="gen27216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27217" type="x-p"/> [1.] He appeals to <hi type="italic">their own sentiments</hi> of this miracle: "<hi type="italic">I have done one work, and you all marvel,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.21">v. 21</reference>. You cannot choose but marvel at it as truly great, and altogether supernatural; you must all own it to be marvellous." Or, "Though I have done but <hi type="italic">one work</hi> that you have any colour to find fault with, yet you marvel, you are offended and displeased as if I had been guilty of some heinous or enormous crime." <div eID="gen27217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27218" type="x-p"/> [2.] He appeals to their own practice in other instances: "<hi type="italic">I have done one work</hi> on the sabbath, and it was done easily, with a word's speaking, and you all marvel, you make a mighty strange thing of it, that a religious man should dare do such a thing, whereas you yourselves <hi type="italic">many a time</hi> do that which is a much more servile work on the sabbath day, in the case of circumcision; if it be lawful for you, nay, and your duty, to circumcise a child on the sabbath day, when it happens to be the eighth day, as no doubt it is, much more was it lawful and good for me to heal a diseased man on that day." Observe, <div eID="gen27218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27219" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The rise and origin of circumcision: <hi type="italic">Moses gave you circumcision,</hi> gave you the law concerning it. Here, 1. Circumcision is said to <hi type="italic">be given,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="John.7.23">v. 23</reference>) they are said to <hi type="italic">receive</hi> it; it was not imposed upon them as a yoke, but conferred upon them as a favour. Note, The ordinances of God, and particularly those which are seals of the covenant, are <hi type="italic">gifts given to men,</hi> and are to be received as such. 2. Moses is said to give it, because it was a part of that law which was <hi type="italic">given by Moses;</hi> yet, as Christ said of the manna (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">ch. vi. 32</reference>), Moses did not give it them, but God; nay, and it was not of Moses first, but <hi type="italic">of the fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.22">v. 22</reference>. Though it was incorporated into the Mosaic institution, yet it was ordained long before, for it was a seal of the righteousness of faith, and therefore commenced with the promise four hundred and thirty years before, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Gal. iii. 17</reference>. The church membership of believers and their seed was not of Moses or his law, and therefore did not fall with it; but was <hi type="italic">of the fathers,</hi> belonged to the patriarchal church, and was part of that blessing of Abraham which was to come upon the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal. iii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen27219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27220" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The respect paid to the law of circumcision above that of the sabbath, in the constant practice of the Jewish church. The Jewish casuists frequently take notice of it, <hi type="italic">Circumcisio et ejus sanatio pellit sabbbatum—Circumcision and its cure drive away the sabbath;</hi> so that if a child was born one sabbath day it was without fail circumcised the next. If then, when the <hi type="italic">sabbath rest</hi> was more strictly insisted on, yet those works were allowed which were <hi type="italic">in ordine ad spiritualia—for the keeping up of religion,</hi> much more are they allowed now under the gospel, when the stress is laid more upon the <hi type="italic">sabbath work.</hi> <div eID="gen27220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27221" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The inference Christ draws hence in justification of himself, and of what he had done (<reference osisRef="John.7.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man-child on the sabbath day receives circumcision, that the law of circumcision might not be broken;</hi> or, as the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">without breaking the law,</hi> namely, of the sabbath. Divine commands must be construed so as to agree with each other. "Now, if this be allowed by yourselves, how unreasonable are you, who are <hi type="italic">angry with me because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day!</hi>" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">emoi cholate</hi></hi>. The word is used only here, from <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">choge</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">fel, gall.</hi> They were angry at him with the greatest indignation; it was a spiteful anger, anger with gall in it. Note, It is very absurd and unreasonable for us to condemn others for that in which we justify ourselves. Observe the comparison Christ here makes between their <hi type="italic">circumcising a child</hi> and his <hi type="italic">healing a man</hi> on the sabbath day. 1. Circumcision was but a ceremonial institution; it was <hi type="italic">of the fathers</hi> indeed, but not from the beginning; but what Christ did was a good work by the law of nature, a more excellent law than that which made circumcision a good work. 2. Circumcision was a <hi type="italic">bloody</hi> ordinance, and <hi type="italic">made sore;</hi> but what Christ did was healing, and made whole. The law works pain, and, if that work may be done on the sabbath day, much more a gospel work, which produces peace. 3. Especially considering that whereas, when they had circumcised a child, their care was only to heal up that part which was circumcised, which might be done and yet the child remain under other illnesses, Christ had made this man <hi type="italic">every whit whole,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">holon anthropon hygie</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I have made the whole man healthful</hi> and sound. The <hi type="italic">whole body</hi> was <hi type="italic">healed,</hi> for the disease affected the whole body; and it was a perfect cure, such as left no relics of the disease behind; nay, Christ not only healed his body, but his soul too, by that admonition, <hi type="italic">Go, and sin no more,</hi> and so indeed made the <hi type="italic">whole man</hi> sound, for the soul is the man. Circumcision indeed was intended for the good of the soul, and to make the <hi type="italic">whole man</hi> as it should be; but they had perverted it, and turned it into a mere carnal ordinance; but Christ accompanied his outward cures with inward grace, and so made them sacramental, and healed the <hi type="italic">whole man.</hi> <div eID="gen27221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27222" type="x-p"/> He concludes this argument with that rule (<reference osisRef="John.7.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.</hi> This may be applied, either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In particular, to this work which they quarrelled with as a violation of the law. Be not partial in your judgment; judge not, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kat opsin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with respect of persons;</hi> knowing faces, as the Hebrew phrase is, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deut. i. 17</reference>. It is contrary to the law of justice, as well as charity, to censure those who differ in opinion from us as transgressors, in taking that liberty which yet in those of our own party, and way, and opinion, we allow of; as it is also to commend that in some as necessary strictness and severity which in others we condemn as imposition and persecution. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In general, to Christ's person and preaching, which they were offended at and prejudiced against. Those things that are false, and designed to impose upon men, commonly appear best when they are judged of <hi type="italic">according to the outward appearance,</hi> they appear most plausible <hi type="italic">prima facie—at the first glance.</hi> It was this that gained the Pharisees such an interest and reputation, that they <hi type="italic">appeared right</hi> unto men (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.27-Matt.23.28">Matt. xxiii. 27, 28</reference>), and men judged of them by that appearance, and so were sadly mistaken in them. "But," saith Christ, "be not too confident that all are real saints who are seeming ones." With reference to himself, his <hi type="italic">outward appearance</hi> was far short of his real dignity and excellency, for he took upon him the <hi type="italic">form of a servant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.7">Phil. ii. 7</reference>), was in the <hi type="italic">likeness of sinful flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>), had <hi type="italic">no form nor comeliness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Isa. liii. 2</reference>. So that those who undertook to judge whether he was the Son of God or no by his <hi type="italic">outward appearance</hi> were not likely to <hi type="italic">judge righteous judgment.</hi> The Jews expected the outward appearance of the Messiah to be pompous and magnificent, and attended with all the ceremonies of secular grandeur; and, judging of Christ by that rule, their judgment was from first to last a <hi type="italic">continual</hi> mistake, for the kingdom of Christ was not to be <hi type="italic">of this world,</hi> nor to <hi type="italic">come with observation.</hi> If a divine power accompanied him, and God bore him witness, and the scriptures were fulfilled in him, though his appearance was ever so mean, they ought to receive him, and to judge by faith, and not by the sight of the eye. See <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">Isa. xi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">and 1 Sam. xvi. 7</reference>. Christ and his doctrine and doings desire nothing but <hi type="italic">righteous judgment;</hi> if truth and justice may but pass the sentence, Christ and his cause will carry the day. We must not judge concerning any by their <hi type="italic">outward appearance,</hi> not by their titles, the figure they make in the world, and their fluttering show, but by their intrinsic worth, and the gifts and graces of God's Spirit in them. <div eID="gen27222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27223" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ discourses with them here concerning <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> whence he came, and whither he was going, <reference osisRef="John.7.25-John.7.36">v. 25-36</reference>. <div eID="gen27223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27224" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Whence he came,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.25-John.7.31">v. 25-31</reference>. In the account of this observe, <div eID="gen27224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27225" type="x-p"/> [1.] The objection concerning this stated by some of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who seem to have been of all others most prejudiced against him, <reference osisRef="John.7.25">v. 25</reference>. One would think that those who lived at the fountain-head of knowledge and religion should have been most ready to receive the Messiah: but it proved quite contrary. Those that have plenty of the means of knowledge and grace, if they are not <hi type="italic">made better</hi> by them, are commonly <hi type="italic">made worse;</hi> and our Lord Jesus has often met with the least welcome from those that one would expect the best from. But it was not without some just cause that it came into a proverb, <hi type="italic">The nearer the church the further from God.</hi> These people of Jerusalem showed their ill-will to Christ, <div eID="gen27225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By their reflecting on the rulers, because they let him alone: <hi type="italic">Is not this he whom they seek to kill?</hi> The multitude of the people that came up out of the country to the feast did not suspect there was any design on foot against him, and therefore they said, <hi type="italic">Who goes about to kill thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.20">v. 20</reference>. But those of Jerusalem knew the plot, and irritated their rulers to put it into execution: "<hi type="italic">Is not this he whom they seek to kill?</hi> Why do they not do it then? Who hinders them? They say that they have a mind to get him out of the way, and yet, lo, <hi type="italic">he speaketh boldly,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they say nothing to him;</hi> do <hi type="italic">the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?</hi>" <reference osisRef="John.7.26">v. 26</reference>. Here they slyly and maliciously insinuate two things, to exasperate the rulers against Christ, when indeed they needed to spur. 1. That by conniving at his preaching they <hi type="italic">brought their authority into contempt.</hi> "Must a man that is condemned by the <hi type="italic">sanhedrim</hi> as a deceiver be permitted to <hi type="italic">speak boldly,</hi> without any check or contradiction? This makes their sentence to be but <hi type="italic">brutem fulmen—a vain menace;</hi> if our rulers will suffer themselves to be thus trampled upon, they may thank themselves if none stand in awe of them and their laws." Note, The worst of persecutions have often been carried on under colour of the necessary support of authority and government. 2. That hereby they brought <hi type="italic">their judgment</hi> into <hi type="italic">suspicion. Do they know that this is the Christ?</hi> It is spoken ironically, "How came they to change their mind? What new discovery have they lighted on? They give people occasion to think that they believe him to be the Christ, and it behoves them to act vigorously against him to clear themselves from the suspicion." Thus the rulers, who had made the people enemies to Christ, made them <hi type="italic">seven times more the children of hell than themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.15">Matt. xxiii. 15</reference>. When religion and the profession of Christ's name are <hi type="italic">out of fashion,</hi> and consequently <hi type="italic">out of repute,</hi> many are strongly tempted to persecute and oppose them, only that they may not be thought to favour them and incline to them. And for this reason apostates, and the degenerate offspring of good parents, have been sometimes worse than others, as it were to wipe off the stain of their profession. It was strange that the rulers, thus irritated, did not seize Christ; but his hour was not yet come; and God can tie men's hands to admiration, though he should not turn their hearts. <div eID="gen27226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27227" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By their exception against his being the Christ, in which appeared more malice than matter, <reference osisRef="John.7.27">v. 27</reference>. "If the rulers think him to be the Christ, we neither can nor will believe him to be so, for we have this argument against it, that <hi type="italic">we know this man, whence he is; but when Christ comes no man knows whence he is.</hi>" Here is a fallacy in the argument, for the propositions are not body <hi type="italic">ad idem—adapted to the same view of the subject.</hi> 1. If they speak of his <hi type="italic">divine nature,</hi> it is true that when Christ comes <hi type="italic">no man knows whence he is,</hi> for he is a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who was <hi type="italic">without descent,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>. But then it is not true that as for this man they knew whence he was, for they knew not his divine nature, nor how <hi type="italic">the Word</hi> was <hi type="italic">made flesh.</hi> 2. If they speak of his <hi type="italic">human nature,</hi> it is true that they knew whence he was, who was his mother, and where he was bred up; but then it is false that ever it was said of the Messiah that none should know whence he was, for it was known before <hi type="italic">where he should be born,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.2.4-Matt.2.5">Matt. ii. 4, 5</reference>. Observe, (1.) How they <hi type="italic">despised him,</hi> because they knew <hi type="italic">whence he was.</hi> Familiarity breeds contempt, and we are apt to disdain the <hi type="italic">use</hi> of those whom we know the <hi type="italic">rise of.</hi> Christ's own received him not, because he was <hi type="italic">their own,</hi> for which very reason they should the rather have loved him, and been thankful that their nation and their age were honoured with his appearance. (2.) How they endeavoured unjustly to fasten the ground of their prejudice upon the scriptures, as if they countenanced them, when there was no such thing. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> people err concerning Christ, because they <hi type="italic">know not the scripture.</hi> <div eID="gen27227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27228" type="x-p"/> [2.] Christ's answer to this objection, <reference osisRef="John.7.28-John.7.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. <div eID="gen27228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27229" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He spoke freely and boldly, he <hi type="italic">cried in the temple, as he taught,</hi> he spoke this louder than the rest of his discourse, 1. To express his earnestness, being <hi type="italic">grieved for the hardness of their hearts.</hi> There may be a vehemency in contending for the truth where yet there is no intemperate heat nor passion. We may instruct gainsayers with warmth, and yet with <hi type="italic">meekness.</hi> 2. The priests and those that were prejudiced against him, did not come near enough to hear his preaching, and therefore he must speak louder than ordinary what he will have them to hear. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear this. <div eID="gen27229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His answer to their cavil is, 1. By way of <hi type="italic">concession,</hi> granting that they did or might know his origin as to the flesh: "<hi type="italic">You both know me, and you know whence I am.</hi> You know I am of your own nation, and one of yourselves." It is no disparagement to the doctrine of Christ that there is that in it which is level to the capacities of the meanest, plain truths, discovered even by nature's light, of which we may say, We know whence they are. "<hi type="italic">You know me,</hi> you think you know me; but you are mistaken; you take me to be the carpenter's son, and born at Nazareth, but it is not so." 2. By way of <hi type="italic">negation,</hi> denying that that which they did see in him, and know of him, was all that was to be known; and therefore, if they looked no further, they judged by the outward appearance only. They knew <hi type="italic">whence</hi> he came perhaps, and <hi type="italic">where</hi> he had his birth, but he will tell them what they knew not, <hi type="italic">from whom</hi> he came. (1.) That he did not <hi type="italic">come of himself;</hi> that he did not run without sending, nor come as a private person, but with a public character. (2.) That he was sent of his Father; this is twice mentioned: <hi type="italic">He hath sent me.</hi> And again, "<hi type="italic">He hath sent me,</hi> to say what I say, and do what I do." This he was himself well assured of, and therefore knew that his Father would bear him out; and it is well for us that we are assured of it too, that we may with holy confidence go to God by him. (3.) That he was <hi type="italic">from his Father,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">par autou eimi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I am from him;</hi> not only sent from him as a servant from his master, but from him by eternal generation, as a son from his father, by essential emanation, as the beams from the sun. (4.) <hi type="italic">That the Father who sent him is true;</hi> he had promised to give the Messiah, and, though the Jews had forfeited the promise, yet he that made the promise is <hi type="italic">true,</hi> and has performed it. He had promised that the Messiah should see his seed, and be successful in his undertaking; and, though the generality of the Jews reject him and his gospel, yet he <hi type="italic">is true,</hi> and will fulfil the promise in the calling of the Gentiles. (5.) That these unbelieving Jews did <hi type="italic">not know the Father: He that sent me, whom you know not.</hi> There is much ignorance of God even with many that have a <hi type="italic">form of knowledge;</hi> and the true reason why people reject Christ is because they do not <hi type="italic">know God;</hi> for there is such a harmony of the divine attributes in the work of redemption, and such an admirable agreement between natural and revealed religion, that the right knowledge of the former would not only admit, but introduce, the latter. (6.) Our Lord Jesus was intimately acquainted with the Father that <hi type="italic">sent him: but I know him.</hi> He knew him so well that he was not at all <hi type="italic">in doubt</hi> concerning his mission from him, but perfectly <hi type="italic">assured</hi> of it; nor at all <hi type="italic">in the dark</hi> concerning the work he had to do, but perfectly <hi type="italic">apprized</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27231" type="x-p"/> [3.] The provocation which this gave to his enemies, who hated him because he <hi type="italic">told them the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.30">v. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">They sought therefore to take him,</hi> to lay violent hands on him, not only to do him a mischief, but some way or other to be the death of him; but by the restraint of an invisible power it was prevented; nobody touched him, <hi type="italic">because his hour was not yet come;</hi> this was not their reason why they did it not, but God's reason why he hindered them from doing it. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The faithful preachers of the truths of God, though they behave themselves with ever so much prudence and meekness, must expect to be hated and persecuted by those who think themselves tormented by their testimony, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God has wicked men in a chain, and, whatever mischief they <hi type="italic">would do,</hi> they <hi type="italic">can do</hi> no more than God will suffer them to do. The malice of persecutors is <hi type="italic">impotent</hi> even when it is most <hi type="italic">impetuous,</hi> and, when Satan <hi type="italic">fills their hearts,</hi> yet God <hi type="italic">ties their hands. Thirdly,</hi> God's servants are sometimes wonderfully protected by indiscernible unaccountable means. Their enemies do not do the mischief they designed, and yet neither they themselves nor any one else can tell why they do not. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Christ had <hi type="italic">his hour</hi> set, which was to put a period to his day and work on earth; so have all his people and all his ministers, and, till that hour comes, the attempts of their enemies against them are ineffectual, and their day shall be lengthened as long as their Master has any work for them to do; nor can all the powers of hell and earth prevail against them, until they have <hi type="italic">finished their testimony.</hi> <div eID="gen27231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27232" type="x-p"/> [4.] The good effect which Christ's discourse had, notwithstanding this, upon some of his hearers (<reference osisRef="John.7.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many of the people believed on him.</hi> As he was set for the fall of some, so for the rising again of others. Even where the gospel meets with opposition there may yet be a great deal of good done, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1 Thess. ii. 2</reference>. Observe here, <hi type="italic">First, Who</hi> they were that believed; not a few, but many, more than one would have expected when the stream ran so strongly the other way. But these <hi type="italic">many</hi> were <hi type="italic">of the people,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek tou ochlou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of the multitude,</hi> the crowd, the inferior sort, the mob, the rabble, some would have called them. We must not measure the prosperity of the gospel by its success among the great ones; nor much ministers say that they labour in vain, though none but the <hi type="italic">poor,</hi> and those of no <hi type="italic">figure,</hi> receive the gospel, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">1 Cor. i. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What <hi type="italic">induced</hi> them to believe: the <hi type="italic">miracles which he did,</hi> which were not only the accomplishment of the Old-Testament prophecies (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6">Isa. xxxv. 5, 6</reference>), but an argument of a divine power. He that had an ability to do that which none but God <hi type="italic">can do,</hi> to control and overrule the powers of nature, no doubt had authority to enact that which none but God can <hi type="italic">enact,</hi> a law that shall <hi type="italic">bind conscience,</hi> and a covenant that shall <hi type="italic">give life. Thirdly,</hi> How <hi type="italic">weak</hi> their faith was: they do not positively assert, as the Samaritans did, <hi type="italic">This is indeed the Christ,</hi> but they only argue, <hi type="italic">When Christ comes will he do more miracles than these?</hi> They take it for granted that Christ will come, and, when he comes, will do many miracles. "Is not this he then? In him we see, though not all the worldly pomp we have fancied, yet all the divine power we have <hi type="italic">believed</hi> the Messiah should appear in; and therefore why may not this be he?" They <hi type="italic">believe</hi> it, but have not courage to own it. Note, Even weak faith may be true faith, and so <hi type="italic">accounted,</hi> so <hi type="italic">accepted,</hi> by the Lord Jesus, who <hi type="italic">despises not the day of small things.</hi> <div eID="gen27232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27233" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Whither he was going,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.32-John.7.36">v. 32-36</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen27233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27234" type="x-p"/> [1.] The design of the Pharisees and chief priests against him, <reference osisRef="John.7.32">v. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The provocation given them was that they had information brought them by their spies, who insinuated themselves into the conversation of the people, and gathered stories to carry to their jealous masters, that <hi type="italic">the people murmured such things concerning him,</hi> that there were many who had a respect and value for him, notwithstanding all they had done to render him odious. Though the people did but whisper these things, and had not courage to speak out, yet the Pharisees were enraged at it. The equity of that government is justly <hi type="italic">suspected</hi> by others which is so <hi type="italic">suspicious</hi> of itself as to take notice of, or be influenced by, the secret, various, uncertain <hi type="italic">mutterings</hi> of the common people. The Pharisees valued themselves very much upon the respect of the people, and were sensible that if Christ did thus <hi type="italic">increase</hi> they must <hi type="italic">decrease. Secondly,</hi> The project they laid hereupon was to seize Jesus, and take him into custody: <hi type="italic">They sent officers to take him,</hi> not to take up those who murmured concerning him and frighten them; no, the most effectual way to disperse the flock is to <hi type="italic">smite the shepherd.</hi> The Pharisees seem to have been the ringleaders in this prosecution, but they, <hi type="italic">as such,</hi> had no power, and therefore they god the <hi type="italic">chief priests,</hi> the judges of the ecclesiastical court, to join with them, who were ready enough to do so.
