The Pharisees were the great pretenders to <hi type="italic">learning,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">chief priests</hi> to <hi type="italic">sanctify.</hi> As <hi type="italic">the world by wisdom knew not God,</hi> but the greatest philosophers were guilty of the greatest blunders in natural religion, so the Jewish church by their wisdom knew not Christ, but their greatest rabbin were the greatest fools concerning him, nay, they were the most inveterate enemies to him. Those wicked rulers had their officers, officers of their court, church-officers, whom they employed to take Christ, and who were ready to go on their errand, though it was an ill errand. If Saul's footmen will not <hi type="italic">turn and fall upon the priests of the Lord,</hi> he has a herdsman that will, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.17-1Sam.22.18">1 Sam. xxii. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen27234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27235" type="x-p"/> [2.] The discourse of our Lord Jesus hereupon (<reference osisRef="John.7.33-John.7.34">v. 33, 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet a little while I am with you, and then I go to him that sent me; you shall seek me, and shall not find me; and where I am, thither you cannot come.</hi> These words, like the pillar of cloud and fire, have a <hi type="italic">bright</hi> side and a <hi type="italic">dark</hi> side. <div eID="gen27235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27236" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They have a <hi type="italic">bright side</hi> towards our Lord Jesus himself, and speak abundance of comfort to him and all his faithful followers that are exposed to difficulties and dangers for his sake. Three things Christ here comforted himself with:—1. That he had but <hi type="italic">a little time</hi> to continue here in this troublesome world. He sees that he is never likely to have a quiet day among them; but the best of it is his warfare will shortly be accomplished, and then he shall be <hi type="italic">no more in this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.11">ch. xvii. 11</reference>. Whomsoever we are <hi type="italic">with</hi> in this world, friends or foes, it is but a <hi type="italic">little while</hi> that we shall be with them; and it is a matter of comfort to those who are <hi type="italic">in</hi> the world, but not <hi type="italic">of</hi> it, and therefore are hated by it and sick of it, that they shall not be <hi type="italic">in it always,</hi> they shall not be <hi type="italic">in it long.</hi> We must be <hi type="italic">awhile</hi> with those that are pricking briars and grieving thorns; but thanks be to God, it is but a little while, and we shall be out of their reach. Our days being <hi type="italic">evil,</hi> it is well they are <hi type="italic">few.</hi> 2. That, when he should quit this troublesome world, he should <hi type="italic">go to him that sent him; I go.</hi> Not, "I am driven away by force," but, "I voluntarily <hi type="italic">go;</hi> having finished my embassy, I return to him on whose errand I came. When I have done my work with you, then, and not till then, I go to him <hi type="italic">that sent me,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">receive me,</hi> will prefer me, as ambassadors are preferred when they return." Their rage against him would not only not hinder him from, but would hasten him to the glory and joy that were set before him. Let those who suffer for Christ comfort themselves with this, that they have a God to go to, and are going to him, going apace, to be for ever with him. 3. That, though they persecuted him here, wherever he went, yet none of their persecutions could follow him to heaven: <hi type="italic">You shall seek me, and shall not find me.</hi> It appears, by their enmity to his followers when he was gone, that if they could have reached him they would have persecuted him: "But you cannot enter into that temple as you do into this." <hi type="italic">Where I am,</hi> that is, where I then <hi type="italic">shall be;</hi> but he expressed it thus because, even when he was on earth, by his divine nature and divine affections he was in heaven, <reference osisRef="John.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>. Or it denotes that he should be <hi type="italic">so soon</hi> there that he was as good as there already. Note, It adds to the happiness of glorified saints that they are out of the reach of the devil and all his wicked instruments. <div eID="gen27236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27237" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> These words have a <hi type="italic">black and dark side</hi> towards those wicked Jews that hated and persecuted Christ. They now longed to be rid of him, <hi type="italic">Away with him from the earth;</hi> but let them know, 1. That according to their choice so shall their doom be. They were industrious to <hi type="italic">drive him</hi> from them, and their sin shall be their punishment; he will not trouble them long, yet a little while and he will <hi type="italic">depart</hi> from them. It is just with God to forsake those that think his presence a burden. They that are weary of Christ need no more to make them miserable than to have <hi type="italic">their wish.</hi> 2. That they would certainly repent their choice when it was too late. (1.) They should in vain seek the presence of the Messiah: "<hi type="italic">You shall seek me, and shall not find me.</hi> You shall expect the <hi type="italic">Christ to come,</hi> but your eyes shall fail with looking for him, and you shall never find him." Those who rejected the true Messiah when he did come were justly abandoned to a miserable and endless expectation of one that should never come. Or, it may refer to the final rejection of sinners from the favours and grace of Christ at the great day: those who now seek Christ shall find him, but the day is coming when those who now refuse him <hi type="italic">shall seek him, and shall not find him.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Prov. i. 28</reference>. They will in vain cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord, open to us.</hi> Or, perhaps, these words might be fulfilled in the despair of some of the Jews, who possibly might be convinced and not converted, who would wish in vain to see Christ, and to hear him preach again; but the day of grace is over (<reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Luke xvii. 22</reference>); yet this is not all. (2.) They should in vain expect a place in heaven: <hi type="italic">Where I am,</hi> and where all believers shall be with me, <hi type="italic">thither ye cannot come.</hi> Not only because they are <hi type="italic">excluded</hi> by the just and irreversible sentence of the judge, and the sword of the angel at every gate of the new Jerusalem, to keep <hi type="italic">the way of the tree of life</hi> against those who have <hi type="italic">no right to enter,</hi> but because they are disabled by their own iniquity and infidelity: <hi type="italic">You cannot come,</hi> because you <hi type="italic">will not.</hi> Those who hate to be where Christ is, in his word and ordinances on earth, are very unfit to be where he is in his glory in heaven; for indeed heaven would be no heaven to them, such are the antipathies of an unsanctified soul to the felicities of that state.
entries.d531c63a5be922051bf563bce363b39ef5f84b6b: <div eID="gen27237" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Gospel Invitation.</title> <div sID="gen27238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> In the last day, that great <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. <hi type="super">38</hi> He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. <hi type="super">39</hi> (But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet <hi type="italic">given;</hi> because that Jesus was not yet glorified.) <hi type="super">40</hi> Many of the people therefore, when they heard this saying, said, Of a truth this is the Prophet. <hi type="super">41</hi> Others said, This is the Christ. But some said, Shall Christ come out of Galilee? <hi type="super">42</hi> Hath not the scripture said, That Christ cometh of the seed of David, and out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was? <hi type="super">43</hi> So there was a division among the people because of him. <hi type="super">44</hi> And some of them would have taken him; but no man laid hands on him. <div eID="gen27238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27239" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen27239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27240" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's discourse, with the explication of it, <reference osisRef="John.7.37-John.7.39">v. 37-39</reference>. It is probable that these are only short hints of what he enlarged upon, but they have in them the substance of the whole gospel; here is a <hi type="italic">gospel invitation to come to Christ,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">gospel promise</hi> of comfort and happiness in him. Now observe, <div eID="gen27240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27241" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">When</hi> he gave this invitation: <hi type="italic">On the last day</hi> of the feast of tabernacles, <hi type="italic">that great day.</hi> The <hi type="italic">eighth day,</hi> which concluded that solemnity, was to be a <hi type="italic">holy convocation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev. xxiii. 36</reference>. Now on this day Christ published this gospel-call, because (1.) Much people were gathered together, and, if the invitation were given to <hi type="italic">many,</hi> it might be hoped that <hi type="italic">some</hi> would accept of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Prov. i. 20</reference>. Numerous assemblies give opportunity of doing the more good. (2.) The people were now returning to their homes, and he would give them this to carry away with them as his parting word. When a great congregation is to be dismissed, and is about to scatter, as here, it is affecting to think that in all probability they will never come all together again in this world, and therefore, if we can say or do any thing to help them to heaven, that must be the time. It is good to be lively at the close of an ordinance. Christ made this offer <hi type="italic">on the last day of the feast.</hi> [1.] To those who had turned a deaf ear to his preaching on the foregoing days of this sacred week; he will try them once more, and, if they will yet hear his voice, they shall live. [2.] To those who perhaps might never have such another offer made them, and therefore were concerned to accept of this; it would be half a year before there would be another feast, and in that time they would many of them be in their graves. <hi type="italic">Behold now is the accepted time.</hi> <div eID="gen27241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27242" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">How</hi> he gave this invitation: <hi type="italic">Jesus stood and cried,</hi> which denotes, (1.) His great earnestness and importunity. His heart was upon it, to bring poor souls in to himself. The erection of his body and the elevation of his voice were indications of the intenseness of his mind. Love to souls will make preachers lively. (2.) His desire that all might take notice, and take hold of this invitation. He <hi type="italic">stood, and cried,</hi> that he might the better be heard; for this is what every one that hath ears is concerned to hear. Gospel truth seeks no corners, because it fears no trials. The heathen oracles were delivered privately by them that <hi type="italic">peeped and muttered;</hi> but the oracles of the gospel were proclaimed by one that <hi type="italic">stood, and cried.</hi> How sad is the case of man, that he must be <hi type="italic">importuned</hi> to be happy, and how wonderful the grace of Christ, that he will <hi type="italic">importune</hi> him! <hi type="italic">Ho, every one,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa. lv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen27242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27243" type="x-p"/> 3. The invitation itself is very general: <hi type="italic">If any man</hi> thirst, whoever he be, he is invited to Christ, be he high or low, rich or poor, young or old, bond or free, Jew or Gentile. It is also very <hi type="italic">gracious: "If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.</hi> If any man desires to be truly and eternally happy, let him apply himself to me, and be ruled by me, and I will undertake to make him so." <div eID="gen27243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27244" type="x-p"/> (1.) The persons invited are such as <hi type="italic">thirst,</hi> which may be understood, either, [1.] Of the <hi type="italic">indigence</hi> of their cases; either as to their <hi type="italic">outward</hi> condition (if any man be destitute of the comforts of this life, or fatigued with the crosses of it, let his poverty and afflictions draw him to Christ for that peace which the world can neither give nor take away), or as to their <hi type="italic">inward</hi> state: "If any man want spiritual blessings, he may be supplied by me." Or, [2.] Of the <hi type="italic">inclination</hi> of their souls and their desires towards a spiritual happiness. If any man hunger and thirst after righteousness, that is, truly desire the good will of God towards him, and the good work of God in him. <div eID="gen27244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27245" type="x-p"/> (2.) The invitation itself: <hi type="italic">Let him come to me.</hi> Let him not go to the ceremonial law, which would neither <hi type="italic">pacify</hi> the conscience nor <hi type="italic">purify it,</hi> and therefore could not make the <hi type="italic">comers thereunto perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">Heb. x. 1</reference>. Nor let him go to the heathen philosophy, which does but beguile men, lead them into a wood, and leave them there; but let him <hi type="italic">go to Christ,</hi> admit his doctrine, submit to his discipline, believe in him; come to him as the fountain of living waters, the giver of all comfort. <div eID="gen27245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27246" type="x-p"/> (3.) The satisfaction promised: "Let him come <hi type="italic">and drink,</hi> he shall have what he comes for, and abundantly more, shall have that which will not only <hi type="italic">refresh,</hi> but <hi type="italic">replenish,</hi> a soul that desires to be happy." <div eID="gen27246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27247" type="x-p"/> 4. A gracious promise annexed to this gracious call (<reference osisRef="John.7.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that believeth on me, out of his belly shall flow</hi>—(1.) See here what it is to come to Christ: It is <hi type="italic">to believe on him, as the scripture hath said;</hi> it is to receive and entertain him as he is offered to us in the gospel. We must not frame a Christ according to our fancy, but believe in a Christ according to the scripture. (2.) See how thirsty souls, that come to Christ, shall be made <hi type="italic">to drink.</hi> Israel, that believed Moses, drank of the <hi type="italic">rock that followed them,</hi> the streams followed; but believers drink of a rock <hi type="italic">in them, Christ in them;</hi> he is in them a <hi type="italic">well of living water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">ch. iv. 14</reference>. Provision is made not only for their <hi type="italic">present</hi> satisfaction, but for their <hi type="italic">continual perpetual</hi> comfort. Here is, [1.] <hi type="italic">Living water, running</hi> water, which the Hebrew language calls <hi type="italic">living,</hi> because still in motion. The graces and comforts of the Spirit are compared to <hi type="italic">living</hi> (meaning <hi type="italic">running</hi>) <hi type="italic">water,</hi> because they are the active quickening principles of spiritual life, and the earnests and beginnings of eternal life. See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jer. ii. 13</reference>. [2.] <hi type="italic">Rivers</hi> of living water, denoting both plenty and constancy. The comfort flows in both <hi type="italic">plentifully</hi> and <hi type="italic">constantly</hi> as a river; strong as a stream to bear down the oppositions of doubts and fears. There is a fulness in Christ of grace for grace. [3.] These flow out <hi type="italic">of his belly,</hi> that is, out of his heart or soul, which is the subject of the Spirit's working and the seat of his government. There <hi type="italic">gracious principles</hi> are planted; and out of the heart, in which the Spirit dwells, flow the <hi type="italic">issues of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.23">Prov. iv. 23</reference>. There divine comforts are lodged, and the <hi type="italic">joy</hi> that a <hi type="italic">stranger doth not intermeddle with. He that believes has the witness in himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.10">1 John v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Sat lucis intus—Light abounds within.</hi> Observe, further, where there are <hi type="italic">springs</hi> of grace and comfort in the soul that will <hi type="italic">send forth streams: Out of his belly shall flow rivers. First,</hi> Grace and comfort will produce good actions, and a holy heart will be seen in a holy life; the tree is known by its fruits, and the fountain by its streams. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They will <hi type="italic">communicate themselves</hi> for the benefit of others; a good man is a common good. His <hi type="italic">mouth</hi> is a <hi type="italic">well of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11">Prov. x. 11</reference>. It is not enough that we <hi type="italic">drink waters out of our own cistern,</hi> that we ourselves take the comfort of the grace given us, but we must let our <hi type="italic">fountains</hi> be <hi type="italic">dispersed abroad,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15-Prov.5.16">Prov. v. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27248" type="x-p"/> Those words, <hi type="italic">as the scripture hath said,</hi> seem to refer to some promise in the Old Testament to this purport, and there are many; as that God would <hi type="italic">pour out</hi> his Spirit, which is a metaphor borrowed from waters (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.23">Prov. i. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joel ii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa. xliv. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>); that the <hi type="italic">dry land</hi> should become <hi type="italic">springs of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">Isa. xli. 18</reference>); that there should be <hi type="italic">rivers in the desert</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.19">Isa. xliii. 19</reference>); that gracious souls should be like a <hi type="italic">spring of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Isa. lviii. 11</reference>); and the church a <hi type="italic">well of living water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.15">Cant. iv. 15</reference>. And here may be an allusion to the waters issuing out of Ezekiel's temple, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Ezek. xlvii. 1</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zech. xiv. 8</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot and others tell us it was a custom of the Jews, which they received by tradition, <hi type="italic">the last day of the feast</hi> of tabernacles to have a solemnity, which they called <hi type="italic">Libatio aquæ—The pouring out of water.</hi> They fetched a golden vessel of water from the pool of Siloam, brought it into the temple with sound of trumpet and other ceremonies, and, upon the ascent to the altar, poured it out before the Lord with all possible expressions of joy. Some of their writers make the water to signify <hi type="italic">the law,</hi> and refer to <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa. xii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">lv. 1</reference>. Others, <hi type="italic">the Holy Spirit.</hi> And it is thought that our Saviour might here allude to this custom. Believers shall have the comfort, not of a vessel of water fetched from a pool, but of a river flowing from themselves. The joy of the law, and the pouring out of the water, which signified this, are not to be compared with the joy of the gospel in the wells of salvation. <div eID="gen27248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27249" type="x-p"/> 5. Here is the evangelist's exposition of this promise (<reference osisRef="John.7.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">This spoke he of the Spirit:</hi> not of any outward advantages accruing to believers (as perhaps some misunderstood him), but of the gifts, graces, and comforts of the Spirit. See how scripture is the best interpreter of scripture. Observe, <div eID="gen27249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27250" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is promised to <hi type="italic">all that believe</hi> on Christ that they shall <hi type="italic">receive the Holy Ghost.</hi> Some received his miraculous gifts (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.17-Mark.16.18">Mark xvi. 17, 18</reference>); all receive his sanctifying graces. The gift of the Holy Ghost is one of the great blessings promised in the new covenant (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Acts ii. 39</reference>), and, if <hi type="italic">promised,</hi> no doubt <hi type="italic">performed</hi> to all that have an interest in that covenant. <div eID="gen27250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27251" type="x-p"/> (2.) The Spirit dwelling and working in believers is as a <hi type="italic">fountain of living</hi> running <hi type="italic">water,</hi> out of which plentiful streams flow, cooling and cleansing as water, mollifying and moistening as water, making them fruitful, and others joyful; see <reference osisRef="John.3.5">ch. iii. 5</reference>. When the apostles spoke so <hi type="italic">fluently</hi> of the things of God, as the Spirit gave them utterance (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.4">Acts ii. 4</reference>), and afterwards preached and wrote the gospel of Christ with such a <hi type="italic">flood</hi> of divine eloquence, then this was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">Out of his belly shall flow rivers.</hi> <div eID="gen27251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> (3.) This plentiful effusion of the Spirit was yet the matter of a promise; for <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.</hi> See here [1.] That <hi type="italic">Jesus was not yet glorified.</hi> It was certain that he should be glorified, and he was ever worthy of all honour; but he was as yet in a state of humiliation and contempt. He had never forfeited the glory he had before all worlds, nay, he had <hi type="italic">merited</hi> a further glory, and, besides his <hi type="italic">hereditary</hi> honours, might claim the <hi type="italic">achievement</hi> of a <hi type="italic">mediatorial</hi> crown; and yet all this is in reversion. Jesus is now <hi type="italic">upheld</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>), is now <hi type="italic">satisfied</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>), is now <hi type="italic">justified</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>), but he is <hi type="italic">not yet glorified.</hi> And, if Christ must wait for his glory, let not us think it much to wait for ours. [2.] That <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost was not yet given.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oupo gar hen pneuma</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for the Holy Ghost was not yet.</hi> The Spirit of God was from eternity, for in the beginning he <hi type="italic">moved upon the face of the waters.</hi> He was in the Old-Testament prophets and saints, and Zacharias and Elisabeth were both <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost.</hi> This therefore must be understood of the eminent, plentiful, and general effusion of the Spirit which was promised, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joel ii. 28</reference>, and accomplished, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Acts ii. 1</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">The Holy Ghost was not yet given</hi> in that visible manner that was intended. If we compare the clear knowledge and strong grace of the disciples of Christ themselves, after the day of Pentecost, with their darkness and weakness before, we shall understand in what sense <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost was not yet given;</hi> the earnests and first-fruits of the Spirit were given, but the full harvest was not yet come. That which is most properly called the <hi type="italic">dispensation of the Spirit</hi> did not yet commence. The <hi type="italic">Holy Ghost</hi> was <hi type="italic">not yet given</hi> in such rivers of living water as should issue forth to water the whole earth, even the Gentile world, not in the <hi type="italic">gifts of tongues,</hi> to which perhaps this promise principally refers. [3.] That the reason why <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost was not given</hi> was because <hi type="italic">Jesus was not yet glorified. First,</hi> The death of Christ is sometimes called his glorification (<reference osisRef="John.13.31">ch. xiii. 31</reference>); for in his cross he conquered and triumphed. Now the gift of the Holy Ghost was purchased by the blood of Christ: this was the <hi type="italic">valuable consideration</hi> upon which the <hi type="italic">grant</hi> was grounded, and therefore till this <hi type="italic">price was paid</hi> (though many other gifts were bestowed upon its being <hi type="italic">secured</hi> to be paid) the Holy Ghost was not given. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There was not so much need of the Spirit, while Christ himself was here upon earth, as there was when he was gone, to supply the want of him. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The giving of the Holy Ghost was to be both an <hi type="italic">answer</hi> to Christ's <hi type="italic">intercession</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">ch. xiv. 16</reference>), and an <hi type="italic">act</hi> of his <hi type="italic">dominion;</hi> and therefore till he is glorified, and enters upon both these, the Holy Ghost is not given. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The conversion of the Gentiles was the glorifying of Jesus. When certain Greeks began to enquire after Christ, he said, <hi type="italic">Now is the Son of man glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>. Now the time when the gospel should be propagated in the nations was not yet come, and therefore there was as yet no occasion for the <hi type="italic">gift of tongues,</hi> that <hi type="italic">river of living water.</hi> But observe, though the Holy Ghost was not yet given, yet he was <hi type="italic">promised;</hi> it was now the great <hi type="italic">promise of the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.4">Acts i. 4</reference>. Though the gifts of Christ's grace are <hi type="italic">long deferred,</hi> yet they are <hi type="italic">well secured:</hi> and, while we are waiting for the good promise, we have the promise to live upon, which <hi type="italic">shall speak and shall not lie.</hi> <div eID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> II. The consequents of this discourse, what entertainment it met with; in general, it occasioned differences: <hi type="italic">There was a division among the people because of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.43">v. 43</reference>. There was a <hi type="italic">schism,</hi> so the word is; there were diversities of opinions, and those managed with heat and contention; various sentiments, and those such as set them at <hi type="italic">variance.</hi> Think we that Christ came to send peace, that all would unanimously embrace his gospel? No, the effect of the preaching of his gospel would be <hi type="italic">division,</hi> for, while some are <hi type="italic">gathered to it,</hi> others will be <hi type="italic">gathered against it;</hi> and this will put things into a <hi type="italic">ferment,</hi> as here; but this is no more the fault of the gospel than it is the fault of a wholesome medicine that it stirs up the <hi type="italic">peccant</hi> humours in the body, in order to the discharge of them. Observe what the debate was:— <div eID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> 1. Some were <hi type="italic">taken with him,</hi> and well affected to him: <hi type="italic">Many of the people, when they heard this saying,</hi> heard him with such compassion and kindness invite poor sinners to him, and with such authority engage to make them happy, that they could not but think highly of him. (1.) Some of them said, <hi type="italic">O, a truth this is the prophet,</hi> that prophet whom Moses spoke of to the fathers, who should be <hi type="italic">like unto him;</hi> or, This is <hi type="italic">the prophet</hi> who, according to the received notions of the Jewish church, is to be the harbinger and forerunner of the Messiah; or, <hi type="italic">This is truly a prophet,</hi> one divinely inspired and sent of God. (2.) Others went further, and said, <hi type="italic">This is the Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.41">v. 41</reference>), not the <hi type="italic">prophet</hi> of the Messiah, but the Messiah himself. The Jews had at this time a more than ordinary expectation of the Messiah, which made them ready to say upon every occasion, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there;</hi> and this seems to be only the effect of some such confused and floating notions which caught at the first appearance, for we do not find that these people became his disciples and followers; a good opinion of Christ is far short of a lively faith in Christ; many give Christ a good word that give him no more. These here said, <hi type="italic">This is the prophet,</hi> and <hi type="italic">this is the Christ,</hi> but could not persuade themselves to leave all and follow him; and so this their testimony to Christ was but a testimony <hi type="italic">against themselves.</hi> <div eID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> 2. Others were <hi type="italic">prejudiced against him.</hi> No sooner was this great truth started, that <hi type="italic">Jesus is the Christ,</hi> than immediately it was contradicted and argued against: and this one thing, that his rise and origin were (as they took it for granted) out of Galilee, was thought enough to answer all the arguments for his being the Christ. For, <hi type="italic">shall Christ come out of Galilee?</hi> Has not <hi type="italic">the scripture said that Christ comes of the seed of David?</hi> See here, (1.) A laudable knowledge of the scripture. They were so far in the right, that the Messiah was to be a <hi type="italic">rod out of the stem of Jesse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>), that out of Bethlehem should <hi type="italic">arise the Governor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>. This even the common people knew by the traditional expositions which their scribes gave them. Perhaps the people who had these scriptures so ready to object against Christ were not alike knowing in other parts of holy writ, but had had these put into their mouths by their leaders, to fortify their prejudices against Christ. Many that espouse some corrupt notions, and spend their zeal in defence of them, seem to be very ready in the scriptures, when indeed they know little more than those scriptures which they have been taught to <hi type="italic">pervert.</hi> (2.) A culpable ignorance of our Lord Jesus. They speak of it as certain and past dispute that <hi type="italic">Jesus was of Galilee,</hi> whereas by enquiring of himself, or his mother, or his disciples, or by consulting the genealogies of the family of David, or the register at Bethlehem, they might have known that he was the Son of David, and a native of Bethlehem; but <hi type="italic">this they willingly are ignorant of.</hi> Thus gross falsehoods in matters of fact, concerning persons and things, are often taken up by prejudiced and partial men, and great resolves founded upon them, even in the same place and the same age wherein the persons live and the things are done, while the truth might easily be found out. <div eID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> 3. Others were <hi type="italic">enraged against him,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">would have taken him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.44">v. 44</reference>. Though what he said was most sweet and gracious, yet they were exasperated against him for it. Thus did our Master suffer ill for saying and doing well. <hi type="italic">They would have taken him;</hi> they hoped somebody or other would seize him, and, if they had thought no one else would, they would have done it themselves. They <hi type="italic">would have taken him;</hi> but no man <hi type="italic">laid hands on him,</hi> being restrained by an invisible power, because his hour was not come. As the malice of Christ's enemies is always <hi type="italic">unreasonable,</hi> so sometimes the suspension of it is <hi type="italic">unaccountable.</hi>
entries.7df387b55d30eb978bcb82ac36e0519f5f65637f: <div eID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Officers' Testimony of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">45</hi> Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him? <hi type="super">46</hi> The officers answered, Never man spake like this man. <hi type="super">47</hi> Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived? <hi type="super">48</hi> Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? <hi type="super">49</hi> But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed. <hi type="super">50</hi> Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,) <hi type="super">51</hi> Doth our law judge <hi type="italic">any</hi> man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth? <hi type="super">52</hi> They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee? Search, and look: for out of Galilee ariseth no prophet. <hi type="super">53</hi> And every man went unto his own house. <div eID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> The chief priests and Pharisees are here in a close cabal, contriving how to suppress Christ; though this was the <hi type="italic">great day of the feast,</hi> they attended not the religious services of the day, but left them to the vulgar, to whom it was common for those great ecclesiastics to consign and turn over the business of devotion, while they thought themselves better employed in the affairs of church-policy. They sat in the council-chamber, expecting Christ to be brought a prisoner to them, as they had issued out warrants for apprehending him, <reference osisRef="John.7.32">v. 32</reference>. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> I. What passed between them and their own officers, who returned without him, <hi type="italic">re infecta</hi>—<hi type="italic">having done nothing.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> 1. The reproof they gave the officers for not executing the warrant they gave them: <hi type="italic">Why have you not brought him?</hi> He appeared publicly; the people were many of them disgusted, and would have assisted them in taking him; this was <hi type="italic">the last day of the feast,</hi> and they would not have such another opportunity; "why then did you neglect your duty?" It vexed them that those who were their own creatures, who depended on them, and on whom they depended, into whose minds they had instilled prejudices against Christ, should thus disappoint them. Note, Mischievous men fret that they cannot do the mischief they would, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.16">Neh. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason which the officers gave for the non-execution of their warrant: <hi type="italic">Never man spoke like this man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.46">v. 46</reference>. Now, (1.) This was a very great truth, that <hi type="italic">never any man spoke with</hi> that wisdom, and power, and grace, that convincing clearness, and that charming sweetness, wherewith Christ spoke; none of the prophets, no, not Moses himself. (2.) The very officers that were sent to take him were taken with him, and acknowledged this. Though they were probably men who had no quick sense of reason or eloquence, and certainly had no inclination to think well of Jesus, yet so much <hi type="italic">self-evidence</hi> was there in what Christ said that they could not but prefer him before all those that sat in Moses's seat. Thus Christ was preserved by the power God has upon the consciences even of bad men. (3.) They said this to their lords and masters, who could not endure to hear any thing that tended to the honour of Christ and yet could not avoid hearing this. Providence ordered it so that this should be said to them, that it might be a vexation in their sin and an aggravation of their sin. Their own officers, who could not be suspected to be biassed in favour of Christ, are witnesses against them. This testimony of theirs should have made them reflect upon themselves, with this thought, "Do we know what we are doing, when we are hating and persecuting one that speaks so admirably well?" <div eID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> 3. The Pharisees endeavour to secure their officers to their interest, and to beget in them prejudices against Christ, to whom they saw them begin to be well affected. They suggest two things:— <div eID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> (1.) That if they embrace the gospel of Christ they will <hi type="italic">deceive themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.47">v. 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">Are you also deceived?</hi> Christianity has, from its first rise, been represented to the world as a great cheat upon it, and they that embraced it as men <hi type="italic">deceived,</hi> then when they began to be <hi type="italic">undeceived.</hi> Those that looked for a Messiah in external pomp thought those deceived who believed in a Messiah that appeared in poverty and disgrace; but the event declares that none were ever more shamefully deceived, nor put a greater cheat upon themselves, than those who promised themselves worldly wealth and secular dominion with the Messiah. Observe what a <hi type="italic">compliment</hi> the Pharisees paid to these officers: "<hi type="italic">Are you also deceived?</hi> What! men of your sense, and thought, and figure; men that know better than to be imposed upon by every pretender and upstart teacher?" They endeavour to prejudice them against Christ by persuading them to think well of themselves. <div eID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they will <hi type="italic">disparage themselves.</hi> Most men, even in their religion, are willing to be governed by the example of those of the <hi type="italic">first rank;</hi> these officers therefore, whose preferments, such as they were, gave them a <hi type="italic">sense of honour,</hi> are desired to consider, <div eID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> [1.] That, if they become disciples of Christ, they go contrary to those who were persons of quality and reputation: "<hi type="italic">Have any of the rulers, or of the Pharisees, believed on him?</hi> You know they have not, and you ought to be bound up by their judgment, and to <hi type="italic">believe</hi> and <hi type="italic">do</hi> in religion according to the will of your superiors; will you be wiser than they?" Some of the rulers did embrace Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Matt. ix. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.53">ch. iv. 53</reference>), and more believed in him, but wanted courage to confess him (<reference osisRef="John.12.42">ch. xii. 42</reference>); but, when the interest of Christ runs low in the world, it is common for its adversaries to represent it as lower than really it is. But it was too true that few, very few, of them did. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The cause of Christ has seldom had rulers and Pharisees on its side. It needs not secular supports, nor proposes secular advantages, and therefore neither courts nor is courted by the great men of this world. <hi type="italic">Self-denial</hi> and the <hi type="italic">cross</hi> are hard lessons to <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and Pharisees. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> This has confirmed many in their prejudices against Christ and his gospel, that the rulers and Pharisees have been no friends to them. Shall <hi type="italic">secular</hi> men pretend to be more concerned about <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> things than spiritual men themselves, or to see further into religion than those who make its study their profession? If <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> do not believe in Christ, they that do believe in him will be the most singular, unfashionable, ungenteel people in the world, and quite out of the way of preferment; thus are people foolishly swayed by <hi type="italic">external motives</hi> in matters of <hi type="italic">eternal moment,</hi> are willing to be damned for fashion-sake, and to go to hell in compliment to the <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees.</hi> <div eID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> [2.] That they will link themselves with the despicable vulgar sort of people (<reference osisRef="John.7.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">But this people, who know not the law, are cursed,</hi> meaning especially those that were well-affected to the doctrine of Christ. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How scornfully and disdainfully they speak of them: <hi type="italic">This people.</hi> It is not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">laos</hi></hi>, this <hi type="italic">lay-people,</hi> distinguished from them that were the clergy, but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ochlos outos</hi></hi>, this <hi type="italic">rabble-people,</hi> this pitiful, scandalous, scoundrel people, whom they disdained to <hi type="italic">set with the dogs of their flock</hi> though God had set them with the lambs of his. If they meant the <hi type="italic">commonalty of the Jewish nation,</hi> they were the seed of Abraham, and in covenant with God, and not to be spoken of with such contempt. The church's common interests are betrayed when any one part of it studies to render the other mean and despicable. If they meant the <hi type="italic">followers of Christ,</hi> though they were generally persons of small figure and fortune, yet by owning Christ they discovered such a sagacity, integrity, and interest in the favours of Heaven, as made them truly great and considerable. Note, As the wisdom of God has often chosen base things, and things which are despised, so the folly of men has commonly debased and despised those whom God has chosen. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How unjustly they reproach them as ignorant of the word of God: <hi type="italic">They know not the law;</hi> as if none knew the law but those that knew it <hi type="italic">from them,</hi> and no scripture-knowledge were current but what came out of their mint; and as if none knew the law but such as were observant of their canons and traditions. Perhaps many of those whom they thus despised <hi type="italic">knew the law,</hi> and the prophets too, better than they did. Many a plain, honest, unlearned disciple of Christ, by meditation, experience, prayers, and especially obedience, attains to a more clear, sound, and useful knowledge of the word of God, than some great scholars with all their wit and learning. Thus David came to understand <hi type="italic">more than the ancients</hi> and <hi type="italic">all his teachers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. If the common people did not <hi type="italic">know the law,</hi> yet the chief priests and Pharisees, of all men, should not have upbraided them with this; for whose fault was it but theirs, who should have <hi type="italic">taught them better,</hi> but, instead of that, <hi type="italic">took away the key of knowledge?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.52">Luke xi. 52</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> How magisterially they pronounce sentence upon them: they are <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> hateful to God, and all wise men; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epikatartoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an execrable</hi> people. It is well that their saying they were cursed did not make them so, for the <hi type="italic">curse causeless shall not come.</hi> It is a usurpation of God's prerogative, as well as great uncharitableness, to say of any particular persons, much more of any body of people, that they are reprobates. We are unable to <hi type="italic">try,</hi> and therefore unfit to <hi type="italic">condemn,</hi> and our rule is, <hi type="italic">Bless, and curse not.</hi> Some think they meant no more than that the people were <hi type="italic">apt to be deceived</hi> and <hi type="italic">made fools of;</hi> but they use this odious word, They are <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> to express their own indignation, and to frighten their officers from having any thing to do with them; thus the language of hell, in our profane age, calls every thing that is displeasing <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">damned,</hi> and <hi type="italic">confounded.</hi> Now, for aught that appears, these officers had their convictions baffled and stifled by these suggestions, and they never enquire further after Christ; one word from a <hi type="italic">ruler</hi> or <hi type="italic">Pharisee</hi> will sway more with many than the true reason of things, and the great interests of their souls. <div eID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> II. What passed between them and Nicodemus, a member of their own body, <reference osisRef="John.7.50">v. 50</reference>, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> 1. The just and rational objection which Nicodemus made against their proceedings. Even in their corrupt and wicked sanhedrim God left not himself quite <hi type="italic">without</hi> witness against their enmity; nor was the vote against Christ carried <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente</hi>—<hi type="italic">unanimously.</hi>Observe, <div eID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> (1.) Who it was that appeared against them; it was Nicodemus, <hi type="italic">he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.50">v. 50</reference>. Observe, concerning him, [1.] That, though he had been with Jesus, and taken him for his teacher, yet he retained his place in the council, and his vote among them. Some impute this to his <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> and cowardice, and think it was his fault that he did not quit his place, but Christ had never said to him, <hi type="italic">Follow me,</hi> else he would have done as others that left all to follow him; therefore it seems rather to have been his <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> not immediately to throw up his place, because there he might have opportunity of serving Christ and his interest, and stemming the tide of the Jewish rage, which perhaps he did more than we are aware of. He might there be as Hushai among Absalom's counsellors, instrumental to <hi type="italic">turn their counsels into foolishness.</hi> Though we must in no case deny our Master, yet we may wait for an opportunity of confessing him to the best advantage. God has his remnant among all sorts, and many times finds, or puts, or makes, some good in the worst places and societies. There was Daniel in Nebuchadnezzar's court, and Nehemiah in Artaxerxes's. [2.] That though at first he came to Jesus <hi type="italic">by night,</hi> for fear of being known, and still continued in his post; yet, when there was occasion, he boldly appeared in defence of Christ, and opposed the whole council that were set against him. Thus many believers who at first were timorous, and ready to <hi type="italic">flee at the shaking of a leaf,</hi> have at length, by divine grace, grown courageous, and able to <hi type="italic">laugh at the shaking of a spear.</hi> Let none justify the disguising of their faith by the example of Nicodemus, unless, like him, they be ready upon the first occasion openly to appear in the cause of Christ, though they stand alone in it; for so Nicodemus did here, and <reference osisRef="John.19.39">ch. xix. 39</reference>. <div eID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he alleged against their proceedings (<reference osisRef="John.7.51">v. 51</reference>): <hi type="italic">Doth our law judge any man before it hear him</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">akouse par autou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">hear from himself</hi>) and <hi type="italic">know what he doeth?</hi> By no means, nor doth the law of any civilized nation allow it. Observe, [1.] He prudently argues from the principles of their own law, and an incontestable rule of justice, that no man is to be condemned <hi type="italic">unheard.</hi> Had he urged the excellency of Christ's doctrine or the evidence of his miracles, or repeated to them his divine discourse with him (<reference osisRef="John.3.1-John.3.21">ch. iii.</reference>), it had been but to <hi type="italic">cast pearls before swine,</hi> who would <hi type="italic">trample them under their feet,</hi> and would <hi type="italic">turn again and rend him;</hi> therefore he waives them. [2.] Whereas they had reproached the people, especially the followers of Christ, as <hi type="italic">ignorant of the law,</hi> he here tacitly retorts the charge upon themselves, and shows how ignorant they were of some of the first principles of the law, so unfit were they to give law to others. [3.] The law is here said to <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">know,</hi> when magistrates that govern and are governed by it <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">know;</hi> for they are the <hi type="italic">mouth of the law,</hi> and whatsoever they bind and loose according to the law is justly said to be bound and loosed by the law. [4.] It is highly fit that none should come under the <hi type="italic">sentence</hi> of the law, till they have first by a fair trial undergone the <hi type="italic">scrutiny</hi> of it. Judges, when they receive the complaints of the accuser, must always reserve in their minds room for the defence of the accused, for they have two ears, to remind them to hear both sides; this is said to be the manner of the Romans, <reference osisRef="Acts.25.18">Acts xxv. 18</reference>. The method of our law is <hi type="italic">Oyer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Terminer,</hi> first to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> and then to <hi type="italic">determine.</hi> [5.] Persons are to be judged, not by what is <hi type="italic">said</hi> of them, but by what they <hi type="italic">do. Our law</hi> will not ask what men's opinions are of them, or out-cries against them, but, What have they done? What <hi type="italic">overt-acts</hi> can they be convicted of? Sentence must be given, <hi type="italic">secundum allegata et probata—according to what is alleged and proved.</hi> Facts, and not faces, must be known in judgment; and the <hi type="italic">scale</hi> of justice must be used before the <hi type="italic">sword</hi> of justice. <div eID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> Now we may suppose that the motion Nicodemus made in the house upon this was, That Jesus should be desired to come and give them an account of himself and his doctrine, and that they should favour him with an impartial and unprejudiced hearing; but, though none of them could gainsay his maxim, none of them would second his motion. <div eID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> 2. What was said to this objection. Here is no direct reply given to it; but, when they could not resist the force of his argument, they fell foul upon him, and what was to seek in <hi type="italic">reason</hi> they made up in railing and reproach. Note, It is a sign of a bad cause when men cannot bear to <hi type="italic">hear reason,</hi> and take it as an affront to be reminded of its maxims. Whoever are <hi type="italic">against reason</hi> give cause to suspect that <hi type="italic">reason</hi> is <hi type="italic">against them.</hi> See how they taunt him: <hi type="italic">Art thou also of Galilee?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.52">v. 52</reference>. Some think he was well enough served for continuing among those whom he knew to be enemies to Christ, and for his speaking no more on the behalf of Christ than what he might have said on behalf of the greatest criminal-that he should not be condemned unheard. Had he said, "As for this Jesus, I have heard him myself, and know he is a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God,</hi> and you in opposing him fight against God," as he ought to have said, he could not have been more abused than he was for this feeble effort of his tenderness for Christ. As to what they said to Nicodemus, we may observe, <div eID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> (1.) How <hi type="italic">false</hi> the grounds of their arguing were, for, [1.] They suppose that Christ was of Galilee, and this was false, and if they would have been at the pains of an impartial enquiry they would have found it so. [2.] They suppose that because most of his disciples were Galileans they were all such, whereas he had abundance of disciples in Judea. [3.] They suppose that out of Galilee no prophet had <hi type="italic">risen,</hi> and for this appeal to Nicodemus's search; yet this was false too: Jonah was of Gath-hepher, Nahum an Elkoshite, both of Galilee. Thus do they <hi type="italic">make lies their refuge.</hi> <div eID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> (2.) How <hi type="italic">absurd</hi> their arguings were upon these grounds, such as were a shame to <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees.</hi> [1.] Is any man of worth and virtue ever the worse for the poverty and obscurity of his country? The Galileans were the seed of Abraham; barbarians and Scythians are the seed of Adam; and <hi type="italic">have we not all one Father?</hi> [2.] Supposing no prophet had risen out of Galilee, yet it is not impossible that any should arise thence. If Elijah was the first prophet of Gilead (as perhaps he was), and if the Gileadites were called <hi type="italic">fugitives,</hi> must it therefore be questioned whether he was a prophet or no? <div eID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27275" type="x-p"/> 3. The hasty adjournment of the court hereupon. They broke up the assembly in confusion, and with precipitation, and <hi type="italic">every man went to his own house.</hi> They met to take <hi type="italic">counsel together against the Lord and his Anointed,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">imagined a vain think;</hi> and not only he that sits in heaven laughed at them, but we may sit on earth and laugh at them too, to see all the policy of the close cabal broken to pieces with one plain honest word. They were not willing to hear Nicodemus, because they could not answer him. As soon as they perceived they had one such among them, they saw it was to no purpose to go on with their design, and therefore put off the debate to a more convenient season, when he was absent. Thus the counsel of the Lord is made to stand, in spite of the devices in the hearts of men.  <chapter eID="John.7"/> <div eID="gen27275" type="x-p"/>

entries.816204c53b4169c6b7678aae86f20946d5667856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15056"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.7.1-John.7.53">Joh 7:1-53</reference>. Christ at the Feast of Tabernacles.</title> <div sID="gen29024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15056"/><hi type="bold">1-2. After these things--</hi>that is, all that is recorded after <reference osisRef="John.5.18">Joh 5:18</reference>.<div eID="gen29024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked in Galilee--</hi>continuing His labors there, instead of going to Judea, as might have been expected.<div eID="gen29025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sought to kill him--</hi>referring back to <reference osisRef="John.5.18">Joh 5:18</reference>. Hence it appears that our Lord did not attend the Passover mentioned in <reference osisRef="John.6.4">Joh 6:4</reference>--being the third since His ministry began, if the feast mentioned in <reference osisRef="John.5.1">Joh 5:1</reference> was a Passover. <div eID="gen29026" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c4e298c3f5c2eddb5d035fb7b6aa3d1e9888b9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15058"/><div sID="gen29028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15058"/><hi type="bold">3-5. His brethren said--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.54-Matt.13.56">Mt 13:54-56</reference>).<div eID="gen29028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Depart ... into Judea, &c.--</hi>In <reference osisRef="John.7.5">Joh 7:5</reference> this speech is ascribed to their unbelief. But as they were in the "upper room" among the one hundred and twenty disciples who waited for the descent of the Spirit after the Lord's ascension (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.14">Ac 1:14</reference>), they seem to have had their prejudices removed, perhaps after His resurrection. Indeed here their language is more that of strong prejudice and suspicion (such as near relatives, even the best, too frequently show in such cases), than from unbelief. There was also, probably, a tincture of vanity in it. "Thou hast many disciples in Judea; here in Galilee they are fast dropping off; it is not like one who advances the claims Thou dost to linger so long here, away from the city of our solemnities, where surely 'the kingdom of our father David' is to be set up: 'seeking,' as Thou dost, 'to be known openly,' those miracles of Thine ought not to be confined to this distant corner, but submitted at headquarters to the inspection of 'the world.'" (See <reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>, "I am become a stranger to my brethren, an alien unto my mother's children!") <div eID="gen29029" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3399e0362b502dba08718c9c1a14f6bbb988f31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15059"/><div sID="gen29030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15059"/><hi type="bold">6-10. My time is not yet come--</hi>that is, for showing Himself to the world.<div eID="gen29030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your time is always ready--</hi>that is "It matters little when we go up, for ye have no great plans in life, and nothing hangs upon your movements. With Me it is otherwise; on every movement of Mine there hangs what ye know not. The world has no quarrel with you, for ye bear no testimony against it, and so draw down upon yourselves none of its wrath; but I am here to lift up My voice against its hypocrisy, and denounce its abominations; therefore it cannot endure Me, and one false step might precipitate its fury on its Victim's head before the time. Away, therefore, to the feast as soon as it suits you; I follow at the fitting moment, but 'My time is not yet full come.'" <div eID="gen29031" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d771057c4f8d1b18941feb961753af86ddba7aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15061"/><div sID="gen29034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15061"/><hi type="bold">11-13. Jews--</hi>the rulers.<div eID="gen29034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sought him--</hi>for no good end.<div eID="gen29035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Where is He?--</hi>He had not been at Jerusalem for probably a year and a half. <div eID="gen29036" type="x-p"/>
entries.2279fefcc8b8e016340d1b686383c57a4252f0a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15064"/><div sID="gen29041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15064"/><hi type="bold">14-15. about the midst of the feast--</hi>the fourth or fifth day of the eight, during which it lasted.<div eID="gen29041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went up into the temple and taught--</hi>The word denotes formal and continuous teaching, as distinguished from mere casual sayings. This was probably the first time that He did so thus openly in Jerusalem. He had kept back till the feast was half through, to let the stir about Him subside, and entering the city unexpectedly, had begun His "teaching" at the temple, and created a certain awe, before the wrath of the rulers had time to break it. <div eID="gen29042" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2abce01244c81353d3c5d8ad0ef8b5337aff894: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15066"/><div sID="gen29045" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15066"/><hi type="bold">16-18. doctrine ... not mine, &c.--</hi>that is, from Myself unauthorized; I am here by commission. <div eID="gen29045" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f251862b00c9134438545649a9b395c4d5e69df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15069"/><div sID="gen29049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15069"/><hi type="bold">19-20. Did not Moses, &c.--</hi>that is, In opposing Me ye pretend zeal for Moses, but to the spirit and end of that law which he gave ye are total strangers, and in "going about to kill Me" ye are its greatest enemies. <div eID="gen29049" type="x-p"/>
entries.3dc76d9a61f568891bad478dad283ecd2de4fa22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15071"/><div sID="gen29051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15071"/><hi type="bold">21-24. I have done one work, &c.--</hi>Taking no notice of the popular appeal, as there were those there who knew well enough what He meant, He recalls His cure of the impotent man, and the murderous rage it had kindled (<reference osisRef="John.5.9">Joh 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.18">16, 18</reference>). It may seem strange that He should refer to an event a year and a half old, as if but newly done. But their present attempt "to kill Him" brought up the past scene vividly, not only to Him, but without doubt to them, too, if indeed they had ever forgotten it; and by this fearless reference to it, exposing their hypocrisy and dark designs, He gave His position great moral strength. <div eID="gen29051" type="x-p"/>
entries.470ae6788ff96183ffc01fa3ffa679ecb3cd5cea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15074"/><div sID="gen29054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15074"/><hi type="bold">25-27. some of them of Jerusalem--</hi>the citizens, who, knowing the long-formed purpose of the rulers to put Jesus to death, wondered that they were now letting Him teach openly. <div eID="gen29054" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbba2f456b81d23f9fc62b7e2db88e93c7a10406: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15077"/><div sID="gen29057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15077"/><hi type="bold">28-29. cried Jesus--</hi>in a louder tone, and more solemn, witnessing style than usual.<div eID="gen29057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye both, &c.--</hi>that is, "Yes, ye know both Myself and My local parentage, and (yet) I am not come of Myself."<div eID="gen29058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he that sent me is true, &c.--</hi>Probably the meaning is, "He that sent Me is the only real Sender of any one." <div eID="gen29059" type="x-p"/>
entries.34764c29e40323f1cf9bf080517914f622b47517: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15078"/><div sID="gen29060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15078"/><hi type="bold">30-32. sought to take ... none laid hands--</hi>their impotence being equal to their malignity. <div eID="gen29060" type="x-p"/>
entries.9400f72543fe1d42b1b68275a3db81f00b304a6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15081"/><div sID="gen29063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15081"/><hi type="bold">33-34. Yet a little while, &c.--</hi>that is, "Your desire to be rid of Me will be for you all too soon fulfilled. Yet a little while and we part company--for ever; for I go whither ye cannot come: nor, even when ye at length seek Him whom ye now despise, shall ye be able to find Him"--referring not to any penitential, but to purely selfish cries in their time of desperation. <div eID="gen29063" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee4285b6396d9eeed1ddccdbc470aa8ecfb08d9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15082"/><div sID="gen29064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15082"/><hi type="bold">35-36. Whither will he go, &c.--</hi>They cannot comprehend Him, but seem awed by the solemn grandeur of His warning. He takes no notice, however, of their questions. <div eID="gen29064" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a658cec53355fd8b01e487adaf15c76ede33415: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15083"/><div sID="gen29065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15083"/><hi type="bold">37-39. the last day, that great day of the feast--</hi>the eighth (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">Le 23:39</reference>). It was a sabbath, the last feast day of the year, and distinguished by very remarkable ceremonies. "The generally joyous character of this feast broke out on this day into loud jubilation, particularly at the solemn moment when the priest, as was done on every day of this festival, brought forth, in golden vessels, water from the stream of Siloah, which flowed under the temple-mountain, and solemnly poured it upon the altar. Then the words of <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Is 12:3</reference> were sung, With joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of Salvation, and thus the symbolical reference of this act, intimated in <reference osisRef="John.7.39">Joh 7:39</reference>, was expressed" [Olshausen]. So ecstatic was the joy with which this ceremony was performed--accompanied with sound of trumpets--that it used to be said, "Whoever had not witnessed it had never seen rejoicing at all" [Lightfoot].<div eID="gen29065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus stood--</hi>On this high occasion, then, He who had already drawn all eyes upon Him by His supernatural power and unrivalled teaching--"Jesus stood," probably in some elevated position.<div eID="gen29066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and cried--</hi>as if making proclamation in the audience of all the people.<div eID="gen29067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink!--</hi>What an offer! The deepest cravings of the human spirit are here, as in the Old Testament, expressed by the figure of "thirst," and the eternal satisfaction of them by "drinking." To the woman of Samaria He had said almost the same thing, and in the same terms (<reference osisRef="John.4.13">Joh 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">14</reference>). But what to her was simply affirmed to her as a fact, is here turned into a world-wide proclamation; and whereas there, the gift by Him of the living water is the most prominent idea--in contrast with her hesitation to give Him the perishable water of Jacob's well--here, the prominence is given to Himself as the Well spring of all satisfaction. He had in Galilee invited all the WEARY AND HEAVY-LADEN of the human family to come under His wing and they should find REST (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>), which is just the same deep want, and the same profound relief of it, under another and equally grateful figure. He had in the synagogue of Capernaum (<reference osisRef="John.6.36">Joh 6:36</reference>) announced Himself, in every variety of form, as "the Bread of Life," and as both able and authorized to appease the "HUNGER," and quench the "THIRST," of all that apply to Him. There is, and there can be, nothing beyond that here. But what was on all those occasions uttered in private, or addressed to a provincial audience, is here sounded forth in the streets of the great religious metropolis, and in language of surpassing majesty, simplicity, and grace. It is just Jehovah's ancient proclamation now sounding forth through human flesh, "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no Money!" &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>). In this light we have but two alternatives; either to say with Caiaphas of Him that uttered such words, "He is guilty of death," or falling down before Him to exclaim with Thomas, " My Lord AND MY God!" <div eID="gen29068" type="x-p"/>
entries.141954d71b9fb2e34bdbaa80cecd0113153768d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15086"/><div sID="gen29076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15086"/><hi type="bold">40-43. Many ... when they heard this ... said, Of a truth, &c.--</hi>The only wonder is they did not all say it. "But their minds were blinded." <div eID="gen29076" type="x-p"/>
entries.4507237e047446fe024c880a51b3362c8342f3df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15089"/><div sID="gen29080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15089"/><hi type="bold">44-49. would have taken him; but, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.7.30">Joh 7:30</reference>). <div eID="gen29080" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca5992f4def8bd027a0ff4cf0c992a7601827c41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15095"/><div sID="gen29089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15095"/><hi type="bold">50-53. Nicodemus--</hi>reappearing to us after nearly three years' absence from the history, as a member of the council, probably then sitting. <div eID="gen29089" type="x-p"/>

entries.6f76b346bd4cd031b3f8d42f17b0129f4d7a3bb7: <div eID="gen41955" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen41956" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41957" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41957" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41956" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41958" type="x-p"/> Jesus continues in Galilee, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.1">Joh 7:1</reference>. He is desired to go to the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.2-Joh.7.5">Joh 7:2-5</reference>. His answer, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.6-Joh.7.9">Joh 7:6-9</reference>. He goes up, and the Jews seek him at the feast, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.10-Joh.7.13">Joh 7:10-13</reference>. He teaches in the temple, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.14-Joh.7.24">Joh 7:14-24</reference>. The Jews are confounded by his preaching, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.25-Joh.7.27">Joh 7:25-27</reference>. He continues to teach; they wish to slay him, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.28-Joh.7.30">Joh 7:28-30</reference>. Many of the people believe on him, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.31">Joh 7:31</reference>. The Pharisees murmur, and our Lord reasons with them, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.32-Joh.7.36">Joh 7:32-36</reference>. His preaching on the last day of the feast, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37-Joh.7.39">Joh 7:37-39</reference>. The people are greatly divided in their opinions concerning him, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.40-Joh.7.44">Joh 7:40-44</reference>. The officers, who were sent by the Pharisees to take him, return, and because they did not bring him, their employers are offended, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.45-Joh.7.49">Joh 7:45-49</reference>. Nicodemus reasons with them, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.50-Joh.7.53">Joh 7:50-53</reference>. <div eID="gen41958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41959" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen41959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41960" type="x-p"/> After these things - St. John passes from the preceding discourse of our Lord, which he delivered a little before the passover, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.4">Joh 6:4</reference>, to the Feast of Tabernacles, which happened six months after, and thus omits many things mentioned by the other evangelists, which our blessed Lord said and did during that time. He had already gone over Galilee four or five times; and he continued there, because he found that the hatred of the Jews was such that they would kill him if they could meet with him in Judea; and his time to suffer was not yet come. <div eID="gen41960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41961" type="x-p"/> For he would not walk in Jewry - Instead of this, some MSS., versions, and fathers read, ουγαρ ειχεν εξουσιαν, he had not authority, or liberty to walk, etc. That is, he was no longer tolerated, and could not preach publicly in Judea, but at the risk of his life. He found greater scope for the exercise of his important ministry in Galilee than in Judea, as the chief priests, etc., were continually plotting his death.
entries.cce30c838251848cf67a6825e916e8b3f7d966f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen41961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41962" type="x-p"/> Feast of tabernacles - This feast was celebrated on the fifteenth day of the month Tisri, answering to the last half of our September, and the first half of October. This month was the seventh of the ecclesiastical, and first of the civil, year. The feast took its name from the tents which were erected about the temple, in public places, in courts, and on the flat roofs of their houses, and in gardens; in which the Jews dwelt for eight days, in commemoration of the forty years during which their fathers dwelt in the wilderness. It was one of the three solemn annual feasts in which all the males were obliged, by the law, to appear at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen41962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41963" type="x-p"/> This feast was celebrated in the following manner. All the people cut down branches of palm trees, willows, and myrtles, (and tied them together with gold and silver cords, or with ribbons), which they carried with them all day, took them into their synagogues, and kept them by them while at prayers. On the other days of the feast they carried them with them into the temple and walked round the altar with them in their hands, singing, Hosanna! i.e. Save, we beseech thee! - the trumpets sounding on all sides. To this feast St. John seems to refer, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">Rev 7:10</reference>, where he represents the saints standing before the throne, with palm branches in their hands, singing, Salvation to God, etc. On the seventh day of the feast, they went seven times round the altar, and this was called Hosanna rabba, the great Hosanna. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.9">Mat 21:9</reference>. But the ceremony at which the Jews testified most joy was that of pouring out the water, which was done on the eighth day of the feast. A priest drew some water out of the pool Siloam, in a golden vessel, and brought it into the temple; and at the time of the morning sacrifice, while the members of the sacrifice were on the altar, he went up and poured this water mingled with wine upon it, the people all the while singing, with transports of joy, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1-Isa.12.6">Isa 12:1-6</reference>, especially <reference osisRef="Isa.12.6">Isa 12:6</reference> : With joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation. To this part of the ceremony, our Lord appears to allude in <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>, of this chapter. <div eID="gen41963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41964" type="x-p"/> During this feast many sacrifices were offered. On the first day, besides the ordinary sacrifices, they offered, as a burnt-offering, thirteen calves, two rams, and fourteen lambs with the offerings of flour and the libations of wine that were to accompany them. They offered also a goat for a sin-offering. On all the succeeding days they offered the same sacrifices, only abating one of the calves each day, so that when the seventh day came, they had but seven calves to offer. On the eighth day, which was kept with greater solemnity than the rest, they offered but one calf, one ram, and seven lambs, for a burnt-offering, and one goat for a sin-offering, with the usual offerings and libations. On this day, they also offered in the temple the first fruits of their latter crops, or of those things which come latest to maturity. During the feast, the 113th, 114th, 115th, 116th, 117th, 118th, and 119th Psalms were sung. Leo of Modena says that, though Moses appointed but eight days, yet custom and the devotion of the people have added a ninth to it, which is called the joy of the law, because that on it they complete the reading of the Pentateuch. See Calmet's Com. and Dict., and father Lamy. For the law relative to this institution, see <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">Lev 23:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev 23:40</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there; and <reference osisRef="Num.29.16">Num 29:16</reference>, etc.
entries.71ffabc16233107e7ea7102cadecbc289c6e7513: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen41964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41965" type="x-p"/> His brethren - said - It is generally supposed that these were the children of the sisters of his mother Mary; but some of the ancients have stated that Joseph had several children by a former wife. See the account of the evangelist prefixed to this Gospel. No solid proof can be alleged against this; nor can we pretend to say that these were not the children of Joseph and Mary. Our blessed Lord, it is true, was her first born, while she was yet a virgin; but no man can prove that he was her last. It is an article of faith, in the Popish Church, to believe in the perpetual virginity of Mary; and in this respect, without any reason, several Protestants seem to be Papists. However this may be, it is certain that the Hebrews gave the name of brethren to all the relatives of a particular family. See <reference osisRef="Gen.31.32">Gen 31:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.46">Gen 31:46</reference>. <div eID="gen41965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41966" type="x-p"/> That thy disciples also may see - That is, the disciples which he had made two years and six months before, at the Passover: <reference osisRef="Joh.2.23">Joh 2:23</reference>.
entries.cca95f473f8497a4bea0875b93e780fdd0a21969: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen41966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41967" type="x-p"/> No man that doeth any thing in secret, etc. - They took it for granted that Christ was influenced by the same spirit which themselves felt; and that therefore he should use every opportunity of exhibiting himself to the public, that he might get into repute; and they hoped that a part of his honor would be reflected back upon themselves, as being his near relations.
